findings.evidence: 2026-10-17 trial onboarding: findings-check --edit exit 0 before F-01, refusal naming C-01.1/C-01.2 after
findings.direct_cause: required() takes classes from the project's own findings and the watch list from their counts; with no findings both are empty.
why: The watch list was designed in a ledger with 121 findings.
No finding is read as nothing to guard against.
findings.root_cause: Missing input was read as success.
findings.sweep: Proposal for the maintainer: below a threshold of own findings, the watch list falls back to a starter set of baseline classes (e.g. C-01, C-02, C-07) so day one is guarded.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-01 detectors feed absent inputs to the product code; the gate's own empty-ledger case was never fed.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: open — a test that an empty ledger still requires the starter questions, once the starter set is decided

findings.title: The ledger books whatever cost the caller states; over MCP the agent reports its own spend
findings.symptom: reserve takes estimatedMaxUsd and settle takes actualUsd from the caller; Sakk has no model field and no price table. Over MCP both numbers come from the agent being gated, so an agent that under-reports keeps spending past the real cap, and one project using several models cannot be priced or broken down per model.
findings.evidence: the maintainer's question 2026-10-17 ('real per-model token prices, or our prediction?'); src/ledger.mjs settle, src/mcp.mjs sakk_reserve/sakk_settle schemas; the REAL gold runner alone takes cost from the vendor CLI's total_cost_usd
findings.direct_cause: The ledger was designed as an amounts book; pricing was left to the caller (README: estimatedMaxUsd is the worst case the provider can bill).
why: The first callers were trusted scripts that know their own prices.
The MCP channel handed the same amount fields to the agent the gate exists to constrain.
findings.root_cause: Input controlled by the gated party crosses into the books unchecked.
findings.instance_fix: open
findings.sweep: Design proposed to the maintainer: a versioned price table per provider/model (unknown model refuses), reserve from model + max tokens, settle from the provider-reported usage, entries carry model, tokens and price version, status breaks spend down per model; later a proxy that reads usage itself and a reconciliation against the provider usage/cost export.
findings.mechanism_gap: The RC-05 detectors check the SHAPE of caller values (prototype names, control characters, paths); none asks whether an amount is the caller's word or a measured figure.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: open — the attack row "under-report actualUsd over MCP" lands with the price table, as a KNOWN row until then

distinct_from.F-193: F-193 is an edit of the stored hot summary after booking, which reserve then trusts; F-125 is the cost the caller states at booking time.

findings.guard: test/claims-are-checked.test.mjs::no user-facing text calls a record signed, immutable or tamper-proof without a mechanism
findings.title: Halt, resume, reconcile and unlock records are called "signed" but carry only a self-declared name
findings.symptom: The CLI help ("(signed)"), README ("signed, global or per agent"), docs/ARCHITECTURE.md ("a signed halt record") and specs/kill-switch/spec.md describe --by records as signed. The code only checks that --by is a non-empty string; anyone can write any name.
findings.evidence: UAE compliance research 2026-10-19 (CBUAE GN §6(f) mapping); bin/sakk.mjs signed() is typeof by === string && by.trim() !== ""
findings.direct_cause: "signed" was used for "carries a name", the word an auditor reads as a cryptographic signature.
why: The halt was designed before identity was in scope.
The docs gate checks that named codes and files exist, not what a word promises.
findings.root_cause: A statement in the docs claims a property the code does not have.
findings.sweep: Replace "signed" with "named" (or "by a named person") in CLI help, README, ARCHITECTURE, specs; real signatures arrive with the approval service (SSO or Sigstore/SSH signing). Done: every user-facing file the new test scans was swept; internal code comments in src/ledger.mjs and test comments still say "signed clearance" and are out of scope (not user-facing, and src/ledger.mjs edits need the money-semantics review).
findings.mechanism_gap: The RC-10 detectors check that named codes, files and counts exist; none checks a security adjective (signed, verified, tamper-proof) against a mechanism.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/claims-are-checked.test.mjs::no user-facing text calls a record signed, immutable or tamper-proof without a mechanism

findings.title: The CBUAE case pack cites a theme the guidance does not contain and omits the binding CBUAE regulations
findings.symptom: cbuae-ai-oversight.json lists "injected-instructions-ignored" under the CBUAE AI Guidance Note, which has no such requirement (closest: §5(d) robustness). The pack anchors only on that non-binding note; the binding Operational Risk Management Regulation C 1/2026 (in force 2026-09-14; Art 12 change management, Art 13 third parties, Art 15 notification) and the Outsourcing Regulation (6.1, 6.3 data outside the UAE) are absent.
findings.evidence: UAE compliance research 2026-10-19 against rulebook.centralbank.ae originals (GN full text; ORM Arts 8–20; Outsourcing Arts 1–8)
findings.direct_cause: The pack was written from summaries of the guidance before any original text was read; the pack itself says THEMATIC and unverified.
why: The blueprint named the guidance note, so the pack followed it.
No one read the CBUAE rulebook before writing the themes.
findings.root_cause: A statement in a pack claims a source the source does not contain.
findings.sweep: Re-anchor the pack on the binding regulations (ORM 8.6, 9.4.5, 12.3/12.5, 13.6–13.9, 15.2–15.3; Outsourcing 5.7/5.8/6.1/6.3; CPS 6.1.6.3) with the GN as supervisory expectation; drop or re-cite the injection theme; check the DIFC and DORA packs the same way; a local law firm signs off before any external use.
findings.mechanism_gap: The pack tests check that verdicts and case ids are consistent and that non-REAL runs cannot read COVERED; nothing checks a theme against the cited source.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: open — every requirement carries a quoted source clause and URL, and a test refuses a requirement without one

findings.title: The CI range check fell back to main on push, so a stacked branch had to answer for files its unmerged parents changed
findings.symptom: PR #15, stacked on #14, went red in the push-event self-evolution job: it demanded answers to C-12.1, C-13.1, C-14.1 and C-16.1 for .claude/settings.json, the workflows and other files that #13 and #14 changed. The pull_request run of the same job, ranged from the PR base, passed.
findings.evidence: CI run 39281845615 (push, failure) vs 39281852992 (pull_request, success), head 26a1bf3; reproduced locally: findings-check --range origin/main lists the four questions, --range origin/evolve/self-evolution exits 0
findings.direct_cause: BASE_REF is empty on push events, and the job defaulted it to main.
why: The job was written and tested on branches cut from main.
A default stood in for a missing input instead of refusing, and nothing ran the job on a stacked branch.
findings.root_cause: An assumption about the environment was never verified.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: the job runs on pull requests only, and an empty base fails instead of falling back to main
findings.guard: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::F-128: the range check runs on pull requests against their own base, with no default
findings.sweep: No other workflow step defaults a missing value (no ":-" in .github/workflows); pr-review.yml checks out the PR base sha explicitly; the local hooks check the working branch, not a base.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-09 detectors vary layouts, git configuration and Node versions for Sakk's own runs; none runs the CI range check on a branch whose base is not main.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::F-128: the range check runs on pull requests against their own base, with no default

distinct_from.F-114: F-114 collects low-impact ledger and release edges that touch ci.yml among other files; F-128 is the self-evolution job defaulting its base to main. Different job, different fix.

findings.title: Answers can be rewritten after review, so what was promised before the change is lost
findings.symptom: The gates read only the final answers file. In a second project running the same loop, about 70 existing answers were rewritten in place after review rounds (2026-10-17 to 10-21); the file still read as written before coding.
findings.evidence: transcript of the sessions that built that project, shell edits to findings/acks/*.yaml replacing answer values after each review round; this repository: findings-check --staged and --range compared nothing against an earlier version
findings.direct_cause: No check compared the committed answers with the ones being committed.
why: Answering before the change was a rule in the docs, checked only as "the file has answers now".
Keeping answers true after a fix looked like hygiene, so rewriting them was the natural move.
findings.root_cause: A required step (answer before you build) was enforced only at one moment, not over time.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: answers files new on a branch are version 2; a committed answer and its guard never change; corrections are appended as revisions naming a finding; pre-commit compares with HEAD and CI walks every commit (R2)
findings.guard: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-129: a committed answer cannot be rewritten at commit time
findings.sweep: Both enforcement points that read answers (pre-commit, CI range) now compare versions; the edit hook needs no comparison because it never accepts a commit.
findings.mechanism_gap: The RC-07 detectors check that gates pass exit codes through and that required steps run; none checks that an input the gate reads cannot be changed after the gate passed.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::an answer, once committed, is never rewritten: corrections are revisions naming a finding

findings.title: The answers check passes any 40 characters of prose, so a class recurs under the very question that was answered
findings.symptom: In the second project, all 91 findings logged since 2026-10-18 whose branch could be identified belong to a class whose question that branch had answered before coding; 73 of 80 upgraded no check. Nothing tied an answer to a check or recorded which answer failed.
findings.evidence: that project's ledger and answers files, counted 2026-10-21 (class of each new finding against the questions answered on its branch); this repository: missingAnswers checked length, placeholders and copies only
findings.direct_cause: An answer was free text; the check could only fail for its form, never for whether it prevents anything.
why: The loop measured "was it answered", the only thing a text check can see.
A miss under an answered question was logged like any other finding, so the loop never learned which answers fail.
findings.root_cause: The check named "the history was considered" but could not fail when it was not applied.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: a version-2 answer names its guard (a test that must resolve at commit and in CI, or "none: <reason>"); a finding introduced on a branch in a class that branch answered must carry answer_failed {qid, why}; the report counts them (R3, R4)
findings.guard: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-130: an answer that names no guard is not an answer
findings.sweep: Applied at all three points that read answers; the report shows the miss rate. Ceiling stated: a guard that resolves can still be too weak (mutation work).
findings.mechanism_gap: The RC-12 detectors check controls, refusal codes and timeouts of product checks; the loop's own answer rule was never asked to fail for its stated reason.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::a finding added under an answered class names the answer that failed

findings.title: Stop-the-line is satisfied by a review document; the next change in a stopped class proceeds as before
findings.symptom: C-02, C-03, C-04, C-13 and C-15 each had two latest escapes with mechanism_upgrade "none", and the gate was green: a review file naming the findings released them.
findings.evidence: test/findings-ledger.test.mjs stop-line test (per root-cause axis, satisfied by text in findings/reviews/); findings-report 2026-10-21: detector upgrade rate 45% (34/76)
findings.direct_cause: The stop-line rule checked for a document, not for a check or a decision.
why: §15.4 was implemented as "write the review", the cheapest observable step.
Nothing refused work in the stopped class, so the review changed nothing downstream.
findings.root_cause: A required step (upgrade the check or stop) existed as a document requirement.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: a stopped class refuses every change that must answer it — hook, pre-commit, CI — until findings/classes.json records a stopline for its latest escape: a detector the class lists and that resolves, a waiver, or debt not yet due (R5)
findings.guard: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-131: a class whose last two escapes upgraded nothing stops the change
findings.sweep: The review requirement stays (it explains); release now needs a stopline record. Debt records proposed for C-04, C-13 and C-15 with dates for the owner to accept.

distinct_from.F-129: F-129 is about answers changing after the gate; F-131 is about the stop-line releasing on a document. Different input, different gate.

findings.mechanism_gap: The RC-07 detectors check that required steps run; the stop-line step was checked by its paperwork.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::a class whose last two escapes upgraded nothing stops changes that must answer it

findings.title: A repository's Claude Code hooks do not run for sessions started in a parent folder
findings.symptom: Claude Code reads .claude/settings.json from the folder a session starts in. Sessions that built the second project started in the parent folder: its pre-edit hook fired 0 times across 228 edit-tool writes to its files (2026-10-17 to 10-21). This repository's hook ran only because the parent folder's settings call it by path.
findings.evidence: hook records in the session transcripts (no PreToolUse output from that project's hook; Sakk hook refusals present); docs/SELF_EVOLUTION.md said "Claude Code sessions also meet the edit hook (.claude/settings.json)" without the condition
findings.direct_cause: The hook was configured where the repository is, and nobody checked where sessions start.
why: The hook was tested by running it directly with a payload, never by observing it fire in a real session.
The loader rule (settings come from the start folder) was not in anyone's model.
findings.root_cause: An assumption about the environment (where hooks are loaded from) was never tried.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: the docs state the loader rule; the Bash check finds this repository from its own location, so a parent folder can route tool calls to it; the parent folder of this workspace now routes PreToolUse and PostToolUse to each repository's own hooks
findings.guard: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-132: a shell write routed from a parent folder still meets the gate
findings.sweep: Both repositories in this workspace with tool hooks are routed by the parent; the other repositories have only session hooks (Stop, Task), which carry no target to route.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-09 detectors vary layouts, git configuration and Node versions for Sakk's own runs; none observes a hook firing from the folder sessions really start in.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::the hook works when the session started in a parent folder

findings.title: The shell gate let git commands that rewrite working-tree files through as read-only
findings.symptom: Independent review of 7237bcb: git checkout -- <file>, git checkout <ref> -- <file>, git restore, git stash pop, git reset --hard and git clean were classified read, so a blocked agent could change or discard tracked files through them without answers; git config <key> <value> (e.g. core.hooksPath) also passed as a read.
findings.evidence: review repro in a harness repo: echo x > src/x.mjs exits 2, git checkout -- src/x.mjs exits 0; classifyShell put checkout, restore, stash, reset, clean in a hand list of "branch moves"
findings.direct_cause: A hand list (GIT_VCS) on the read-only side admitted subcommands that write files.
why: The rule "provably read-only" was applied to commands by name, and git was listed by subcommand name without asking what each does to the working tree.
The classifier table tested git reads and branch creation but no git subcommand that writes.
findings.root_cause: A list stood in for the rule on the side that lets things through.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: git is classified by what each command does to the working tree — pathspec checkouts, restore and rm/mv are writes with targets; stash push/pop/apply, reset --hard/--merge/--keep, clean, cherry-pick, revert, apply and config writes are opaque; only commands that create or move between existing commits pass
findings.guard: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-133: git commands that rewrite tracked files are writes
findings.sweep: Every git subcommand the classifier names was re-read for its effect on tracked files; npm install now names package.json and package-lock.json; npm ci, which writes only ignored files, passes.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-02 detectors check docs, bundle keys and suite environments; the new classifier table was itself the detector and listed no git writes.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::the shell classifier: every read-only form passes and every writing form is caught

answer_failed.why: The answer said the gate states one rule (provably read-only) instead of listing commands, but the read side was itself a hand list of git subcommands, and its guard table had no git write to fail on.

findings.title: Renaming the branch started a fresh answers file, so committed answers could be rewritten
findings.symptom: Independent review of 7237bcb: after git branch -m feat/y feat/y2, a new findings/acks/feat-y2.json with contradicting answers passed --staged and --range; the frozen answers under the old name were no longer consulted.
findings.evidence: review repro in a harness repo; --range compared only the current branch's answers file across commits
findings.direct_cause: A missing earlier version (no file under the new name) was read as "nothing to compare".
why: The freeze was keyed on the branch name, which the author controls.
The absence of a previous version was treated as a new branch rather than checked against the other answers files the range had added.
findings.root_cause: Absence of the earlier answers was read as success.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: the range check freezes every answers file the range added; the current file must carry each one's answers forward unchanged (revisions may be appended)
findings.guard: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-134: renaming the branch does not unfreeze committed answers
findings.sweep: pre-commit cannot see the range base, so the rename is caught in CI; the docs state it.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-01 detectors delete inputs to the product code and the empty-ledger case; the answers freeze was tested only under one branch name.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::renaming the branch does not unfreeze its answers (review I2)

answer_failed.why: The answer listed every new input that refuses when absent, but not the earlier answers file, whose absence under a new branch name read as a fresh start.

findings.title: A later escape with any upgrade text released a stopped class
findings.symptom: Independent review of 7237bcb: a third escape whose mechanism_upgrade was any string not starting with "none:" (e.g. "x") released a stopped class with no stopline record and no check that resolves.
findings.evidence: review probe of stoppedClasses with a third escape mechanism_upgrade "x" → no stopped classes
findings.direct_cause: The release path counted the absence of the "none:" prefix, not a check that resolves.
why: The detector path required a reference that resolves; the later-escape path was written as the negation of "none" and never given the same test.
The ledger gate checks resolution, but the hook and commit check run without it.
findings.root_cause: One of two release paths could not fail for the reason it names.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: an escape counts as upgraded only when its mechanism_upgrade is a path::name that resolves
findings.guard: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-135: a later escape with a prose upgrade does not release a stopped class
findings.sweep: Both release paths (stopline record, later escape) now resolve the reference with the same function.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-03 detectors check refusal codes and controls; the stop-line's two release paths were tested one at a time.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::a later escape releases a stopped class only with an upgrade that resolves (review I3)

answer_failed.why: The answer said a stopped class needs a detector that resolves; that held for the stopline record but not for release by a later escape, which nothing tested.

findings.title: A guard could point at a document or the answers file and still count as a check
findings.symptom: Independent review of 7237bcb: guards such as findings/acks/feat-y.json::C-01.1, docs/SELF_EVOLUTION.md::answer and README.md::hello passed the format check and resolved.
findings.evidence: review probe of guardProblem and resolveRef
findings.direct_cause: A guard was accepted when its file existed and contained the name, whatever the file was.
why: The rule was written for the shape path::name, not for what the path is.
The tests used test files only, so nothing tried a document.
findings.root_cause: Evidence that a check exists was accepted from a source that is not a check.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: a guard path must be a test (a test folder, or a .test/.spec/_test/test_ file name) and never under findings/ or a document type
findings.guard: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-136: a guard must be a test, not a document
findings.sweep: Answers and revisions share the same guard rule; stop-line detectors were already restricted to class detectors.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-06 detectors check bundle modes and model metrics; the answers' new evidence field was not given a source rule.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::every answer names a guard that resolves, or says none with a reason

answer_failed.why: The answer said an answer must point at a test that resolves, but the code accepted any file containing the name, and no test tried a document.

findings.title: The data the gate reads could be loosened in the same change it judges
findings.symptom: A branch could delete or reword a prevention question, drop a class detector, delete a finding or move its status back, and the gate then judged the branch by the loosened data. Replaying the ledger history found one silent rewrite: commit f0bb305 changed F-63.symptom with no record.
findings.evidence: R6 replay over the 19 commits that touched findings/ledger.json or findings/classes.json between main and this branch (2026-10-21)
findings.direct_cause: The checker read the head's classes and ledger without comparing them to the base.
why: "Classes only grow" and "a finding's account of the past is fixed" were rules in prose.
The checker trusted its inputs because they live in the same repository.
findings.root_cause: A required property of the gate's own inputs existed only as rule text.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: findings-check compares the ledger and the registry with HEAD (pre-commit) and with the base (CI): nothing is removed, frozen fields change only with a correction record, status moves forward, questions are only appended to, detectors only grow (R6)
findings.guard: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-137: a prevention question cannot be loosened in the change it judges
findings.sweep: Both data files the gate reads are covered at both comparison points; the one historical rewrite (F-63.symptom, f0bb305) predates the rule and stays as history.
findings.mechanism_gap: The RC-07 detectors check that gates run and pass exit codes through; none checks that the gate's inputs cannot be weakened by the change being judged.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::the registry and the ledger only move forward between base and head (R6)

findings.title: CI ran the pull request's own checker, so a branch could loosen the check that judged it
findings.symptom: The self-evolution job checked out the pull request and ran its scripts/findings-check.mjs; a branch that replaced the checker with "exit 0" passed its own CI.
findings.evidence: reproduced in a throwaway repository: the gutted checker exits 0 on a change with no answers; the base's checker, read with git show, exits 1
findings.direct_cause: The judge was the version of the checker the author had just written.
why: On pull_request, GitHub runs the branch's workflow and the branch's files.
Nothing compared the checker's verdict with the verdict of the version already merged.
findings.root_cause: The writer of the change also supplied its judge.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: a CI step reads the base branch's checker scripts with git show and runs them over the branch too; both must pass
findings.guard: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-138: CI runs the base branch's checker over every pull request
findings.sweep: The workflow file itself is still the branch's on pull_request; moving the base-checker run to a workflow the branch cannot edit is the next step (pull_request_target or a ruleset-required workflow), tracked in the hardening plan.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::the base branch's checker judges the pull request too
findings.mechanism_gap: The RC-12 detectors check the product's checks (controls, refusal codes, timeouts); none asked whether the loop's own checker could be replaced by the change it judges.

findings.title: No guard was ever shown to fail before its fix
findings.symptom: A finding's guard only had to exist and pass. Run on the code before their fixes, all 11 guards of F-120…F-138 failed only because the test file could not load (it imports what the fix added); none failed by its own assertion, so none showed the old code had the bug.
findings.evidence: scripts/findings-proof.mjs over release/oss-prep..evolve/hardening, 2026-10-21: 11 of 11 "cannot load before the fix"
findings.direct_cause: Nothing ran a guard on the code before the fix.
why: The ledger gate checks that a guard resolves and passes now; passing now says nothing about before.
Guards were written as unit tests of new functions, which cannot run on code that lacks them.
findings.root_cause: The check that a fix is guarded could not fail for the reason it names.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: CI runs findings-proof (R7): each guard fails on the base with the new test copied in and passes on the branch; an old bug needs a guard that fails there by its own assertion; the guards of F-120…F-138 now drive the checker as a command (test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs)
findings.guard: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-139: a guard that already passes before the fix is refused
findings.sweep: All findings fixed in this pull-request series re-pointed to command-level guards and re-proven; earlier findings are proven when they are next touched.
findings.mechanism_gap: The RC-12 detectors check product checks and the gate's own refusals; none ran a guard against the code before its fix.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution-cli.test.mjs::F-139: a guard that already passes before the fix is refused

findings.title: The shell gate let git commands that turn the hooks off through, and offered no legitimate way to dispute a gate
findings.symptom: git commit --no-verify, git commit -n, git push --no-verify, git -c core.hooksPath=… and git config core.hooksPath passed the Claude Code shell gate once the answers existed (commit and push count as recording, not writing). A blocked agent had no sanctioned alternative to routing around the gate.
findings.evidence: anthropics/claude-code#40117 (Mar 2026): an agent used --no-verify across six commits despite memory and CLAUDE.md rules; ImpossibleBench (arXiv 2510.20270): giving agents an abort/flag option cut cheating from 54% to 9% for GPT-5; reproduced here on the evolve/close-bypasses checker
findings.direct_cause: The classifier judged git commit and push by whether they write files, not by whether they switch the hooks off.
why: Skipping hooks was treated as acceptable because CI re-checks the branch, but CI runs only on pull requests and work before a PR is unchecked.
Refusals said what to answer, never what to do when the gate itself is wrong.
findings.root_cause: A required step (run the hooks) could be skipped by a flag, and the only alternative to complying was to route around.

findings.title: The broken-checker window and the loop classifier trusted inputs they should have resolved or refused

findings.evidence: adversarial review of the gate and CI, 2026-10-22 (findings 4, 5, 6, and the node --test note); scripts in scratchpad/rev
findings.direct_cause: Each input was taken at face value: a path by its leaf, a payload by a key, a thrown value as an Error, a node flag list as harmless.
why: The window realpath-resolved only the parent directories, not the leaf.
The thrown value was assumed to be an Error with a .message.
node was assumed read-only whenever its first argument was --test, without reading the injecting flags.
findings.root_cause: The gate trusted the shape of its inputs instead of resolving or validating them.

findings.title: sakk ledger verify claimed an intact history but never checked the index, and false-failed on float drift
findings.symptom: The adversarial review of the F-105 archive found the cold trail's audit was not what it claimed: (1) HIGH — the call-id index is the only cross-history duplicate guard, but sakk ledger verify walked only the segment chain, so a lost index shard silently re-admitted a sealed call-id (a double-spend) and verify still reported SOUND; (2) the segment chain is an unkeyed sha256 with its tip in the writable hot file, so verify's 'intact and unaltered' wording over-claimed — it detects accidental corruption and loss, not a writer who recomputes the hashes; (3) LOW — verify folded the settled total per entry while maybeSeal accumulated it per segment, so float non-associativity could make an intact chain fail its own audit; (4) LOW — sakk ledger export --out failed with a raw Node stack instead of a typed code.
findings.evidence: independent adversarial review of oss/f105-archive, 2026-10-22 (HIGH index loss, MEDIUM unauthenticated chain, two LOW); reproductions r1-index-loss, r2-float-drift, r3-tamper, r4-export-out
findings.direct_cause: verify checked the chain but not the index, and recomputed the total in a different order than it was stored.
why: The index was treated as a derived cache, so the audit that vouches for the history did not include it.
The recompute and the maintained summary used different float-summation orders with a fixed absolute tolerance.
The audit's wording promised tamper-evidence the unkeyed, hot-anchored chain cannot give.
findings.root_cause: An audit named a guarantee (intact, unaltered, no reused call-id) stronger than what it actually checked.

answer_failed.why: C-03.1 asks whether a check fails for the reason it names and only that; verify named integrity of the whole history but did not check the index (missed a double-spend), over-claimed tamper-evidence, and could false-fail on an intact chain from float order.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: verify also rebuilds the expected index from cold and fails if any sealed call-id is missing or wrong; reserve refuses when segments are sealed but the whole index is gone; sakk ledger reindex rebuilds it; verify sums the total per segment exactly as maybeSeal does (no float false-fail); the spec states verify detects accidental corruption and loss, not tampering by a writer who can recompute the unkeyed hashes; export --out wraps its write error as a typed LEDGER_EXPORT_FAILED.
findings.guard: test/ledger-archive.test.mjs::verify catches a lost index, and reserve refuses rather than re-admit a sealed call-id
findings.sweep: verify now covers both the chain and the index; the reserve-time wholesale-loss guard and reindex give a fail-closed path and a recovery; the float summation matches in both places; the spec and CLI no longer claim tamper-evidence the design does not provide (out-of-band signing is a named later milestone).
findings.mechanism_gap: The archive tests checked the chain (flipped byte, broken link, wrong tip) but never a lost index, and the integrity claim was not read back against what verify actually walked.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/ledger-archive.test.mjs::verify catches a lost index, and reserve refuses rather than re-admit a sealed call-id

findings.title: The M3 secret guard fell open on a zero-action command and on cursor's non-Write write surfaces
findings.symptom: The independent adversarial review of the M3 secret guard found two fail-open gaps and a test-matrix hole: (1) MEDIUM — the secret deny was emitted only inside the per-action loop, so a command that tokenizes to zero actions (a comment-only command, or a bare NAME=<secret> assignment) produced no decision and the call defaulted to allow, contradicting the stated invariant 'a secret found is always a deny'; (2) MEDIUM — write content was captured for claude-code's Write/Edit/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit and for cursor's Write, but not cursor's Edit/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit, which fell through to kind 'other' with no content, so a secret written through those cursor tools was never scanned; (3) MEDIUM — the ack claimed each write surface and agent was 'exercised', but the tests drove only Write/Edit/Bash under claude-code, and MUT-AK mutated only the secretHit call-site, not the loop placement or the normalize surface capture; (4) LOW — the ceiling text did not name the MultiEdit-join and Edit-old/new seams, and a DEFENSIVE note over-stated that the scan-error trigger was tested.
findings.evidence: independent adversarial review of oss/m3-secret-guard at 7d0ea44, 2026-10-22; probes: a zero-action command carrying a secret allowed (before), a cursor Edit carrying a secret allowed (before); no HIGH — no live secret written to disk or sent to the network was allowed in normal operation.
findings.direct_cause: The guarantee 'a secret is always denied' was emitted per action, so an empty action set emitted nothing; and content capture was wired per known (agent, tool) pair, so the cursor non-Write write tools had no capture.
why: The secret deny was written as one more branch inside the per-action loop, inheriting the loop's 'no action -> no decision -> allow' default.
The write surfaces were added one (agent, tool) pair at a time rather than as one 'every write surface, every agent' rule, so a cell was left empty.
The tests and the drill mirrored the pairs that were wired, so the empty cells and the zero-action shape were never driven and the gap stayed invisible until review.
findings.root_cause: A call-level invariant — a secret is always denied, on every write surface and every agent — was implemented as scattered per-route checks and exercised only on the routes that happened to be wired.

answer_failed.why: C-01.1 asks that absence never read as a pass; a zero-action command (absence of a classified action) and an unwired cursor write surface (absence of captured content) both read as allow although a secret was present.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: the secret deny is now a call-level floor — if a secret is found and the per-action loop emitted no decision, a deny is recorded anyway; cursor's Edit/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit capture content exactly as Write does; new tests drive every write surface (MultiEdit, NotebookEdit), the codex apply_patch body, the cursor Edit surface, and the zero-action command, each with a no-secret control; the ack's C-09 wording now matches what the tests exercise; the spec names the split-across-seams ceiling and the DEFENSIVE note no longer claims the scan-error trigger is unit-tested.
findings.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::a command that tokenizes to zero actions still cannot carry a secret
findings.sweep: the floor denies any zero-action secret-bearing call for every agent, and the surface tests now cover every write tool and the codex and cursor agents, so a future regression that drops a surface or the normalize capture goes red. No follow-up needed: both gaps and the test-matrix hole are closed in this commit.
findings.mechanism_gap: RC-01's detectors catch unknown-argument fail-open (cli-strictness) and absent/unreachable checks (claims-are-checked), but none drove the secret guard with a zero-action command or a cursor edit, and MUT-AK mutated only the secretHit call-site, not its placement inside the per-action loop or the normalize surface capture.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::a command that tokenizes to zero actions still cannot carry a secret

findings.title: M2's CHANGELOG documented sakk spend / cap / prices CLI commands that the binary never implemented
findings.symptom: Preparing the M5 release, a docs-vs-code cross-check found that M2's CHANGELOG describes `sakk spend`, `sakk cap set` / `sakk cap off`, `sakk prices` and `sakk prices update` as shipped commands, but bin/sakk.mjs has no such commands — M2 shipped the spend/prices libraries (src/spend.mjs, src/prices.mjs) and the hook's cap enforcement (reading ~/.sakk/config.json), not the CLI surface. A user who followed the CHANGELOG to run `sakk cap set` would get a usage error, and there is no shipped way to set the cap except hand-editing config.json. No check compared a documented `sakk <command>` against the commands the CLI actually implements, so the overclaim passed the gate.

findings.direct_cause: The CHANGELOG was written to the intended spend/cap CLI surface rather than to what bin/sakk.mjs actually implemented, and the claims-check only compared backticked error codes and file names, never command names.
why: The spend/cap feature was split — the library and the hook enforcement shipped, the CLI surface did not — and the CHANGELOG described the whole intended feature as done.
The C-05 detectors (claims-are-checked) verify that named error codes and backticked file names exist, but no detector asked whether a documented `sakk <command>` is a real subcommand.
So a release note could promise a command the binary did not have, and nothing failed.
findings.root_cause: The docs stated a capability (a CLI command) the code did not provide, and the honesty detectors did not cover documented commands, only codes and file names.

answer_failed.why: C-05.1 asks that every sentence added to docs is backed by something that fails without it; the M2 CHANGELOG's command sentences were backed by nothing — the commands did not exist and no test checked that they did.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: the M2 CHANGELOG section is rewritten to shipped reality (the daily cap is enforced by the hook from ~/.sakk/config.json, spend is viewable in sakk ui, and the dedicated spend/cap/prices CLI is marked not shipped and pending a product decision); test/release.test.mjs adds a detector that every `sakk <command>` named in a code span of the README or CHANGELOG is a real subcommand (read from bin) or an explicitly declared PLANNED one. findings.title: The console's read-only /api/agents ran subprocesses and could block the event loop; four lower review notes
findings.symptom: The independent review of M4 found: (1) MODERATE — GET /api/agents called doctor() with its default probe, which spawnSync-fires every installed hook and mkdir's Sakk's home, so a request labelled read-only executed subprocesses and, because spawnSync is synchronous, could stall the single-threaded server for up to (installed hooks x 15 s) — violating the spec's read-only and bounded-work guarantees. Behind the token gate, so not web-reachable, and the console's own tests never installed a hook, so the spawn path was never exercised. A latent bug rode along: the console passed SAKK_HOME where doctor expects the OS home, so it would have looked for agent configs in the wrong place. (2) LOW — GET /api/overview called updateIndex, writing the spend index on a read. (3) LOW — the halt response said 'name typed by the user' though the name is the OS account, auto-derived. (4) LOW — the spec claimed the token cookie was 'scoped to that port', which HTTP cookies are not. (5) LOW — CSV export did not neutralise leading = + - @ (spreadsheet formula injection).
findings.evidence: independent adversarial review of oss/m4-console at b821cf9, 2026-10-22; the reviewer noted /api/agents returned in 48 ms only because the fixture had no installed hook, so the spawnSync path was untested.
findings.direct_cause: The read-only endpoint reused doctor(), a CLI function that fires the installed hook and creates Sakk's home, instead of a read-only variant; the cost-bounds detector bounds each exported function alone and did not see doctor composed into an HTTP GET.
why: doctor() was written for the CLI, where firing the hook and creating the home are wanted; the console reused it unchanged for a GET.

The C-04 detector proves each exported function is bounded in isolation, but nothing checked that a bounded-for-the-CLI function stays bounded and side-effect-free when wired behind a read-only HTTP route.
The console's tests installed no hook, so the fire-on-GET path and the wrong-home bug never ran.
findings.root_cause: A read-only, bounded surface reused a function built to act (fire a subprocess) and to write, and no check caught the composition because the cost detector looks at functions one at a time.

answer_failed.why: C-04.1 asks what bounds the work on hostile input; /api/agents' work was (installed hooks x spawnSync 15 s) of blocking subprocess time, unbounded by any counter or refusal — and it was not read-only.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: doctor() gains probe:false — it reports each hook's installed state without firing it or creating the home; the console calls doctor({probe:false}) and passes the OS home (fixing the wrong-home bug); /api/overview no longer calls updateIndex, so a GET writes nothing (the hook maintains the index); the halt note now reads 'self-declared (the OS account name, not a verified identity)'; the spec no longer claims a port-scoped cookie; CSV export prefixes a leading = + - @ with a quote. A test installs a hook and asserts /api/agents reports it installed without firing.
findings.guard: test/console.test.mjs::the agents page reports installed hooks without firing them (read-only, bounded)
findings.sweep: the agents endpoint is the only place the console reused an acting function; it now uses the read-only probe, and the test that installs a hook guards the no-fire path. The other four notes are each fixed and the read-only guarantee now holds for every GET. No follow-up finding needed.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-04 cost-bounds detector binds every exported function to a proof of its own bound, but doctor's proof was 'run by a person against the agent's config, never on the hook path' — true for the CLI; the detector had no way to see the console had wired doctor into a read-only HTTP GET, where firing subprocesses is neither read-only nor bounded.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/console.test.mjs::the agents page reports installed hooks without firing them (read-only, bounded)

findings.title: A one-command symlink/hard-link chain let an agent reach ~/.sakk, defeating the static path guard
findings.symptom: The spend/cap CLI review found that the shipped claim 'the agent cannot raise its own cap' was false: a single Bash command 'ln -s $SAKK_HOME lnk && echo {"capUsd":999999} > lnk/config.json' was silently allowed and raised the cap. The guard classifies paths by resolving the nearest existing parent at classify time; the symlink does not exist yet, so lnk/config.json resolves to the cwd (allowed), and the link is only followed at run time (a TOCTOU). The same route let the agent clobber any ~/.sakk state (the decision log, the kept-good policy), not just the cap. A hard link (ln target y) and cp -s/-l do the same; the two-command form was already denied (the link exists on the second call), and direct Write/Edit/redirect/cp/mv to ~/.sakk were all denied.
findings.evidence: independent review of oss/spend-cli at b5030a6, 2026-10-22: the chained symlink command returned a silent allow and config.json read capUsd 999999 after run; the two-call form and all direct routes were denied.
findings.direct_cause: The classifier resolves a path through the nearest EXISTING parent; a link created earlier in the same command does not exist at classify time, so the write through it resolves to a safe scope instead of the link's real target.
why: Path scoping is a static resolution of what exists now; a symlink or hard link created mid-command is a future alias the static resolver cannot follow.
The guard's C-08 tests covered a link to an existing target (the ledger path), never a link CREATED and then used within one command.
The spend/cap test exercised only the Write tool for the 'cannot set its own cap' claim, so the shell/link route was never driven and the gap shipped as an absolute claim.
findings.root_cause: A path-based guard resolved a name to a scope using the filesystem state at classify time, so a name aliased at run time by a link the same command creates reached a different, protected target than the one judged.

answer_failed.why: C-08.1 asks whether the same thing can be reached by two names and requires one name to be the only one; a chained link gave ~/.sakk a second name the static resolver did not follow, so a protected path was reached under an unjudged alias.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: a command that creates a link (ln, or cp -s/-l) AND has more than one segment is treated as shell.constructed — it needs a person's approval, never a silent allow, because the guard cannot follow a link that does not exist yet. A standalone link-create is unchanged (a later separate command re-resolves the now-existing link and is denied). The claim is softened to 'cannot silently raise its own cap', and the test now drives the symlink and hard-link routes, not only Write.
findings.guard: test/spend-cli.test.mjs::the agent cannot set its own cap (writing ~/.sakk is denied)
findings.sweep: the fix covers both link kinds (symbolic and hard) and cp's link flags, chained via && ; | or newlines; a standalone link-create stays allowed and its later use is caught on the next call. Residual (accepted, documented): a person can still approve the chained command — human-in-loop, not a silent agent bypass. No follow-up finding needed.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-08 symlink/hard-link detectors resolved a link to an EXISTING target at classify time (F-85, the ledger path); none considered a link created earlier in the SAME command, whose target does not exist yet, so the static resolver scoped the alias as safe.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/spend-cli.test.mjs::the agent cannot set its own cap (writing ~/.sakk is denied)

distinct_from.F-85: F-85 is a ledger reached through a symlink/hard link that ALREADY EXISTS (resolved and refused at classify time); F-163 is a link the command CREATES before using it, which the static resolver cannot follow — a run-time TOCTOU, closed by treating a chained link-create as constructed.
distinct_from.F-173: F-163 is a filesystem-link TOCTOU — the command CREATES a symlink/hard-link then uses it, so the static resolver follows pre-create state to a different target; it mutates the filesystem between classify and open. F-173 mutates nothing: the secret already exists under its real name; the shell merely expands a glob/brace/variable so the written token never spells the path the OS opens. Both are classify-view ≠ run-target, but one is a link race, the other lexical expansion.

findings.title: The gitleaks port emitted (?-i:…) scopes that only Node 23+ compiles, so the whole CLI crashed at import on Node 20 and 22
findings.symptom: CI on oss/gitleaks-port (Node 20 and 22) failed: importing src/secret-scan.mjs threw 'Invalid regular expression … Invalid group' while compiling etsy-access-token, so every test that loads the scanner — and every sakk command — crashed. Locally (Node 25) the port, its compile check and the whole suite passed.
findings.evidence: CI run on PR #26 (jobs test (20), test (22)); reproduced locally with node --no-js-regexp-modifiers bin/sakk.mjs --version (throws at src/secret-scan.mjs:96); four generated rules carried (?-i:: etsy-access-token, generic-api-key, hashicorp-tf-api-token, sumologic-access-token.
findings.direct_cause: translate() refused an unknown inline group only if it was the FIRST '(?' match in the pattern; these rules start with a plain (?: group, so the later (?-i: was never checked, and the fallback compile check ran on the developer's Node 25, which has regexp modifiers.
why: The refusal check used String.match (first hit only), so any pattern with an earlier (?: group skipped the check entirely.
The last line of defence — 'it must compile as a Node RegExp' — compiled on whatever Node ran the port, which locally is the newest one, not the floor (engines >= 20).
The answer to C-09.1 said the regexes are compiled on the Node the project targets; nothing in the local gate runs that Node, so the answer was true only in CI.
findings.root_cause: A check that the output runs on the supported runtime was performed on the newest runtime, so syntax the floor lacks passed every local check; only the CI matrix runs the floor.

answer_failed.why: C-09.1 claimed the generated regexes are compiled on Node 20+, but the test compiled them on the local Node 25; a construct only Node 23+ accepts passed every local run.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: (?-i:…) inside a (?i) pattern is translated by dropping the i flag and case-folding everything outside the scope (the scope is copied verbatim as (?:…)); every '(?' opener — not only the first — must be one Node 20 has or the rule is refused. Three rules that were refused for the same scope (authress, okta, sumologic-access-id) now port too: 194 ported, 192 enabled, 1 refused. Verified with node --no-js-regexp-modifiers: the CLI loads and all 205 generated regexes compile.
findings.guard: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::every generated regex uses only syntax Node 20 has, and (?-i:…) keeps its meaning (F-164)
findings.sweep: Other generated or hand-written regexes that could carry Node-23-only syntax: the guard test reads every generated rule and allowlist regex from the text (inline flag groups and repeated group names); the hand-written rules in src/secret-scan.mjs and src/classify.mjs have no inline flag groups (grep '(?[a-z-]*[:)]'). Duplicate named groups were checked with --no-js-regexp-duplicate-named-groups: the CLI loads.
findings.mechanism_gap: Second occurrence after F-121 of 'passes only on the newest Node': the local gate runs one Node version, and the port's compile check inherited it. F-121's upgrade was 'none, CI catches it'; that held again, but only after a push.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/gitleaks-port.test.mjs::every generated regex uses only syntax Node 20 has, and (?-i:…) keeps its meaning (F-164)

distinct_from.F-121: F-121 is a test that overflowed JSON.stringify on older V8 (a runtime behaviour difference in test code); F-164 is generated product code using syntax older V8 rejects at compile time, which broke the shipped CLI, not only a test.

findings.title: A spend test passed only on 2026-10-22: its logs were dated that day while the hook read the real clock
findings.symptom: From 2026-10-23 the commit gate on oss/gitleaks-port failed test/spend.test.mjs 'the cap denies inside the hook's evaluate' ('allow' !== 'deny'). The same test fails on the unmodified branch head, and every branch from oss/m2-spend up carries it, so each CI re-run from that day on goes red.
findings.evidence: Local gate on 2026-10-23 (Asia/Dubai, 09:44Z): the one failure in the full run; reproduced alone with node --test --test-name-pattern='cap denies inside' on a clean checkout of 57e5958.
findings.direct_cause: The test wrote a session log stamped 2026-10-22T10:00Z and called evaluate() without its now option, so the hook took Date.now() as 'today' and the logged spend fell on yesterday.
why: Every capCheck test in the file passed now: NOW, but the two that go through evaluate() did not; evaluate defaults now to Date.now.
The test was written and first run on 2026-10-22, the only day its fixtures and the real clock agree, so it passed every local and CI run that day.
Nothing checks that a test with dated fixtures also fixes the clock the code under test reads.
findings.root_cause: A test assumed the day it runs equals the day its fixtures are stamped; the code took its clock from the environment, and that other environment (any later day) was never tried.

answer_failed.why: C-09.2's guard is the very test that broke: it drove the cap through evaluate(), the real path, but left evaluate's clock real while its logs were dated, so it was true only on 2026-10-22 and no run on another day had tried it.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: both evaluate() calls in test/spend.test.mjs pass now: () => NOW, the log's mtime is set to NOW, and the test also asserts the same logs allow on the next day — the hook's clock, not the run date, decides 'today'. Product code was right: evaluate passes now() to the cap check.
findings.guard: test/spend.test.mjs::the cap denies inside the hook's evaluate, not only in capCheck
findings.sweep: Every evaluate() and capCheck() call in test/spend.test.mjs is read by the new detector (all now carry now). The other suites that call evaluate() configure no cap, so the run date does not reach a decision; the full gate on 2026-10-23 had this as its only failure.
findings.mechanism_gap: No check tied dated fixtures to a fixed clock; the suite was green on the day it was written and so could not show the dependency.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/spend.test.mjs::every hook or cap call in the spend tests sets its own clock (F-165)

distinct_from.F-62: F-62 is a stopwatch deciding pass/fail under load (C-04, a duration); F-165 is a calendar date assumed equal to the run date (C-09), which fails deterministically from the next day.

findings.title: The drill CI job outgrew its fixed 45-minute limit, so CI cancelled it and PRs #23-#26 read red
findings.symptom: On PRs #23-#26 the drill job (Node 20 and 22) was cancelled at 45 minutes: npm run drill alone took 2653-2705 s, against 1681-1845 s on #20. A cancelled required job reads as a failed check, so a correct branch could not show green CI.
findings.evidence: GitHub Actions step timings: #20 drill 1845 s / 1681 s; #23 drill 2653 s (cancelled) and 2178 s (passed) on two runs; #24 drill 2679 s and 2705 s (both cancelled). The fuzz and campaign steps after it take under 35 s.
findings.direct_cause: scripts/mutation-drill.sh reruns a whole npm test script for each of its 38 mutants; the M4 console and M5 release tests made each rerun about 71 s on CI, and 38 x 71 s passed the 45-minute timeout-minutes set by hand when the suite was smaller.
why: The drill copies the repo and runs the full suite per mutant, so its cost is mutants x suite time.
The suite grew in M2-M5 (spend, console, release tests), raising the per-mutant time from about 45 s to about 71 s on CI.
The job limit was a fixed number of minutes, and no check related it to the number of mutants or to measured run time, so the limit was crossed only when CI cancelled the job.
findings.root_cause: A cost that grows with the work (mutants x suite) was bounded only by a hand-set clock limit in the workflow, with nothing tying that limit to the work it has to cover.

answer_failed.why: C-04.1 was answered for the console code (log tail and request size bounded by counters), not for the cost the new tests add to CI, where the drill reruns the suite per mutant and only the 45-minute clock bounded it.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: the drill job timeout-minutes is 75 (needs 64 at 100 s per mutant for 38 mutants; observed about 45 minutes); test/claims-are-checked.test.mjs adds a check that the drill limit covers the mutant count at a declared per-mutant budget, so adding mutants without raising the limit fails.
findings.guard: test/claims-are-checked.test.mjs::the drill job has time for every mutant it runs (F-166)
findings.sweep: The other CI jobs (test 30 min, format, self-evolution, base-checker 10 min) run once per push and finished well inside their limits on every run checked (#19-#26), so the drill is the only instance. Not done here (no class fix claimed): the per-mutant budget is a measured figure and goes stale as the suite grows; a class fix would run each mutant against only the test file that holds its named killer, so per-mutant cost stops growing with the suite and CI minutes drop. That changes the drill itself and is left for the release checklist.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-04 detectors bound the product code by counters (cost-bounds, bounded-spawn, test timeouts) but none looked at the CI drill, whose work scales with the mutant count and was bounded only by a fixed clock.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/claims-are-checked.test.mjs::the drill job has time for every mutant it runs (F-166)

distinct_from.F-62: F-62 is a stopwatch deciding a test result under load; F-166 is a CI job limit that did not scale with the work the job runs, so the job was cancelled rather than judged.

findings.title: The certificate witness drifted from the drill: EXPECTED_MUTANTS stayed 26 and the freshness regex matched only single-letter ids, so a genuinely all-green drill of 38 mutants could not be certified
findings.symptom: The first real `npm run certificate` on the stack refused with CERT_STALE_EVIDENCE (kills=38 checked=26 expected=26) although every one of the 38 mutants was killed, both control suites were green, and the tree was clean. A correct release state could not produce a certificate.
findings.evidence: mutation-drill-report.txt: 38 'MUTANT KILLED' lines and 38 MUT blocks (26 single-letter MUT-A..MUT-S, 12 two-letter MUT-AA..MUT-AL); 'DRILL PASS: 38/38'. gate-certificate.mjs had `const EXPECTED_MUTANTS = 26` and the freshness regex `/\[(MUT-[A-Z])\] .../` whose single-letter class cannot match a two-letter id. scripts/mutation-drill.sh defines 38 run_drill calls.
findings.direct_cause: The freshness regex MUT-[A-Z] matched only the 26 single-letter ids, so verifyDrillFreshness returned checked=26 against kills=38 and the checked===kills completeness guard (F3) made fresh=false; EXPECTED_MUTANTS was also still 26.
why: The drill grew from 26 to 38 mutants during M1-M5 (MUT-AA..MUT-AL added for archive, hook, console and release paths).
The witness hardcoded the 26-mutant single-letter world in two places (EXPECTED_MUTANTS and the hash-freshness regex) and neither was updated when the drill grew.

Nothing linked the drill's real mutant count or its id shape to the witness at test time; only a full certificate run (minutes, rarely invoked) exercised the witness, so the divergence stayed invisible until the first real run — the same shape as F-149, where a drill property was checked only by the drill itself.

Latent severity (C-01): had the F3 completeness guard not existed, the single-letter regex would have been absence-read-as-success, issuing a certificate while the 12 two-letter mutants' tampered-file freshness went unverified. Defense in depth contained it as a false refusal instead of a false certificate.
findings.root_cause: The witness that must track the drill (its mutant count and id shape) was kept in sync by nothing but the rarely-run certificate itself; no test fails at `npm test` time when the drill and the witness diverge.

answer_failed.why: When the drill grew past 26 mutants, C-10.1 ('make a test fail when the step is missing') was not honored for the witness: the new mutants were added to the drill and the CI timeout was raised (F-166), but no test tied the drill's actual count or id shape to EXPECTED_MUTANTS or to the freshness regex, so the witness could drift untested.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: EXPECTED_MUTANTS is moved to module scope, exported, and set to 38; the freshness regex is widened to MUT-[A-Z]+ so every two-letter id is in reach of hash verification; test/certificate.test.mjs adds three tests that read scripts/mutation-drill.sh, assert its run_drill id count equals EXPECTED_MUTANTS, and drive verifyDrillFreshness with the drill's real id set so checked must equal the full count.
findings.guard: test/certificate.test.mjs::EXPECTED_MUTANTS equals the number the drill actually defines
findings.sweep: The other two hardcoded-count/shape couplings between the drill and its readers were checked: the drill's anchors are already linked to their files by F-149 (core-specs.test.mjs), and the drill's CI time budget to its mutant count by F-166 (claims-are-checked.test.mjs). This finding closes the third — the certificate witness. No class fix claimed: EXPECTED_MUTANTS stays a conscious tripwire deliberately not derived from the drill, so a drill that silently shrinks still fails the count-link test rather than silently lowering the expectation.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-10 detectors turn rule text into checks for the product and (F-149) for the drill's anchors, but none tied the certificate witness's expected mutant count or its id-parsing regex to the drill it testifies about; that coupling was exercised only by the certificate run itself.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/certificate.test.mjs::the freshness parser can see every mutant id the drill emits (the MUT-AA regex gap)

distinct_from.F-149: F-149 made the drill's per-file anchors checkable without running the drill; F-167 makes the drill's mutant count and the witness's id-parsing reach checkable without running the certificate. Same mechanism (a drill property checked only by the drill/cert), different property and different reader.
distinct_from.F-166: F-166 is the drill's CI time budget not scaling with the mutant count (C-04, a clock); F-167 is the certificate witness's expected count and id regex not tracking the mutant set (C-10, an untested coupling). Both stem from the 26->38 growth but on different readers.

findings.title: costOf reads an empty cache_creation:{} split as an authoritative zero, charging nothing for cache-write tokens the same usage would be billed for without the split key
findings.symptom: A usage row with cache_creation_input_tokens:1000 and an empty cache_creation:{} object is priced at $0 for those 1000 cache-write tokens, while the identical row without the split key is priced at 1000×cacheWrite5m. The spend ledger silently undercounts (underbills) whenever a provider or a replayed log emits an empty breakdown object.
findings.evidence: probe: costOf(entry,{cache_creation_input_tokens:1000, cache_creation:{}}) === 0 vs costOf(entry,{cache_creation_input_tokens:1000}) === 0.00375 (entry.cacheWrite5m = 3.75/M). src/prices.mjs costOf: `let w5=cacheWrite,w1h=0; if (split && typeof split==='object'){ w5=count(split,'ephemeral_5m_input_tokens'); w1h=count(split,'ephemeral_1h_input_tokens'); }` — an empty {} is truthy and typeof 'object', so w5/w1h are overwritten with 0. Pinned by test/spend.test.mjs 'GAP F-168 S-FN-012 ...'.
findings.direct_cause: costOf treats the presence of a cache_creation object as proof that it carries the full 5m/1h breakdown; an empty object passes the `split && typeof split===object` guard and zeroes w5 and w1h, discarding the cache_creation_input_tokens total it would otherwise have charged.
why: The cache_creation split was added to price the 5m and 1h ephemeral tiers separately, assuming that whenever the object is present it enumerates the breakdown.

A provider, or a replayed/trimmed log, can emit cache_creation:{} — the key present but empty — which the guard reads as "the breakdown is all zero" rather than "no breakdown was given, fall back to the aggregate".
The empty-object branch was never exercised; only populated splits and the no-key path were tested, so the absence of a breakdown inside a present object read as success (zero cost).
findings.root_cause: A present-but-empty breakdown object is accepted as a complete, authoritative breakdown; the code checks that the split key exists but never that it actually carries the tokens it is trusted to account for.
findings.sweep: Swept: the only other split consumer, parseLine cache_creation normalization in src/spend.mjs, always writes both ephemeral fields (0 when absent) and never emits an empty object, and its sub-counts are now integer-screened (tokenCount), so costOf never sees a non-integer or an authoritative-looking empty split from a parsed line.
findings.mechanism_gap: The RC-01 detectors verify assumptions on the surfaces they were written for (ledger reserve/settle, policy byte-matching, the certificate witness); none drives costOf cache_creation branch, so the assumption that a present split object is a complete split was outside every existing detector reach.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/spend.test.mjs::F-168 S-FN-012 empty cache_creation:{} falls back to the aggregate cache-write

distinct_from.F-170: F-170 is a malformed (non-integer) count that is not screened or isolated and crashes pricing; F-168 is a well-formed row whose empty cache split is silently priced at zero. Opposite failure modes — unhandled crash vs silent undercount.
distinct_from.F-180: F-180 is a charge the price model has no kind for (per-request server tools); F-168 was a priced token kind, cache writes, dropped by an empty breakdown.

findings.instance_fix: this commit: costOf (src/prices.mjs) honours the cache_creation split only when it enumerates tokens (s5 + s1h > 0); a present-but-empty object falls back to the aggregate cache_creation_input_tokens, so cache-write tokens are no longer silently zeroed. test/spend.test.mjs now asserts the empty-split cost equals the no-split cost and that a populated split is still priced per-tier.
findings.guard: test/spend.test.mjs::F-168 S-FN-012 empty cache_creation:{} falls back to the aggregate cache-write

findings.title: A fractional token count passes parseLine finiteNonNeg validation, then throws USAGE_INVALID deep in costOf, and daySpend does not isolate the throw — so `sakk spend` crashes instead of failing closed cleanly
findings.symptom: A usage row with a non-integer count (e.g. input_tokens:1.5) is accepted and stored by parseLine, then crashes daySpend/capCheck with an unhandled USAGE_INVALID PriceError when costOf is reached. `sakk spend` aborts rather than marking the line unreadable and denying with a readable reason.
findings.evidence: probe/test: parseLine(...usage:{input_tokens:1.5}) returns the row with usage.input_tokens === 1.5 (src/spend.mjs validates with finiteNonNeg, not an integer check); daySpend({...}) then throws /USAGE_INVALID/ because costOf count() rejects the non-integer. daySpend calls costOf with no try/catch, so the throw is not isolated to an unreadable-line path. Pinned by test/spend.test.mjs 'GAP F-170 S-SEC-004 ...'.
findings.direct_cause: parseLine token validation (finiteNonNeg) accepts fractional values, so a non-integer survives into the day index; costOf count() then throws USAGE_INVALID, and daySpend has no per-line guard to turn that throw into an unreadable-line deny, so it propagates and crashes the command.
why: parseLine was written to reject negative and non-finite counts but not non-integer ones, so a fractional token is treated as valid input and stored.
The integer invariant lives only in costOf count(), far from the parse boundary, and it signals by throwing rather than by a value parseLine could screen on.

daySpend trusts that every stored, parsed line can be priced and calls costOf without isolating a per-line failure, so a single malformed row aborts the whole command rather than reading as one unreadable line.
findings.root_cause: A malformed token count is neither screened at the parse boundary nor isolated where it is priced; the integer requirement is enforced only by a throw deep in costOf that no caller catches, so an invalid row aborts the command instead of failing closed as one unreadable line.

findings.title: An agent that may run the `sakk` binary can lift its own daily cap (cap off / cap set) and remove its own kill switch (guard uninstall) with no named-human gate — the very controls meant to bind it
findings.symptom: The daily cap and an installed guard are safety controls meant to hold against the agent. halt/resume/reconcile/unlock all refuse without --by <name>, but `sakk cap off`, `sakk cap set <huge>` and `sakk guard uninstall claude-code` succeed (exit 0) with no named human and no confirmation: the cap is deleted or raised to any value, and the PreToolUse hook file removes itself. An agent permitted to run `sakk` can disable the ceiling and the kill switch it is supposed to be bound by.
findings.evidence: test: test/kill-switch.test.mjs 'GAP J-UAT-016 ...' drives the real CLI in an isolated HOME/SAKK_HOME/cwd — `sakk halt` without --by exits 2 (named-human gate), while `cap off` / `cap set 999999` / `guard uninstall claude-code` each exit 0 and change state (capUsd removed, capUsd=999999, .claude/settings.json no longer carries the sakk hook). The same test feeds `sakk cap off` through the REAL hook evaluate(): none of the dedicated protections (halt/spend-cap/secret) fire, so running the self-disable over Bash is not caught by the guard it tears down. bin/sakk.mjs:705 asserts in a comment 'the agent is denied writing ~/.sakk, so it cannot raise its own cap' — but the sakk binary writes config.json itself; that write is not a classified Bash file-write the hook denies.
findings.direct_cause: The cap and guard admin subcommands call writeConfig / guard-install directly and carry no --by requirement, and the hook does not classify an invocation of the sakk binary as the protected-home write it performs; so the only barrier the design assumes (the hook denying a Bash write to ~/.sakk) is bypassed by the sakk binary doing the write on the agent's behalf.
why: The named-human gate (--by) was added to the controls that were framed as human overrides — halt, resume, reconcile, unlock — but cap and guard were framed as operator setup, so the same gate was never written for them.

The cap design assumed the agent can only change config by a Bash file-write to ~/.sakk, which the hook denies; it did not account for the agent invoking the sakk binary, which performs that write itself and is not classified as a protected-home mutation.

The admin surface was only exercised on the happy path (a human runs cap/guard and it works); it was never driven adversarially as the agent disabling its own controls, so the missing authorization boundary never surfaced.
findings.root_cause: The authorization boundary that keeps a control out of the hands of the actor it constrains is applied inconsistently: halt-family subcommands demand a named human, but the cap and guard subcommands trust whoever runs the binary, and the hook does not treat running sakk-admin as crossing into the protected home — so the agent sits on the untrusted side of the cap/guard boundary yet can move both.
findings.sweep: Swept every sakk subcommand that writes Sakk's state, the ledger or an agent's hook config. init, scan --install-hook and guard install only tighten (they add a cap, a ledger link or a hook and never replace a recorded one), so the CLI leaves them ungated; guard install is still asked by the hook as an agent-config write. Every form of cap is now denied to the agent by the hook, and its loosening forms need a person at a terminal; the pseudo-terminal drivers that could answer that prompt (script, expect, unbuffer) are asked by the hook. One more control the agent can lift turned up: resume, reconcile and unlock trust a self-declared --by, the hook lets an agent run them, and the default ledger is an in-repo file the agent may write — filed as F-177, because fixing it needs a decision on where the ledger lives and which policy scope names it.
findings.mechanism_gap: The RC-05 detectors defend the trust boundary on the content/model surfaces they were written for (a writer repeating injected instructions, a judge decoding and scoring base64); none treats the agent itself as the untrusted party at the CLI admin boundary, so an agent invoking sakk to disable its own cap and guard was outside every existing RC-05 detector.

findings.title: A halt never reaches the installed hook in a default install: `sakk halt` writes the ledger to a cwd-relative path while the hook reads halt only from config.ledgerPath ?? SAKK_LEDGER_PATH, and no command writes config.ledgerPath — so the kill switch is silently inert
findings.symptom: After `sakk init --cap N` then `sakk halt --by <name>` in a project, the installed PreToolUse hook (node sakk.mjs hook --agent <agent>) does NOT honor the stop. haltFor resolves the ledger from config.ledgerPath ?? env.SAKK_LEDGER_PATH, neither of which is set out of the box, so it returns {known:false, halt:null}: the agent keeps running with no deny and no error. The operator pulled the kill switch and nothing stopped.
findings.evidence: test test/kill-switch.test.mjs 'GAP J-UAT-030 ...' drives the real CLI and real hook in an isolated HOME/SAKK_HOME/cwd: `sakk init --cap 100` then `sakk halt --by alice` write ./sakk-ledger.json in cwd; evaluate(normalize('claude-code', <Bash `rm -rf build` event>), {env}) in the default install produces NO decision with ruleId 'halt', while the same call with env.SAKK_LEDGER_PATH pointed at the written ledger is denied by ruleId 'halt' (verdict deny). src/hook.mjs:426 `haltFor(ev.agent, config.ledgerPath ?? env.SAKK_LEDGER_PATH)` and :262-263 `if (!ledgerPath) return {known:false, halt:null}`; bin/sakk.mjs:79 the CLI resolves `--ledger ?? SAKK_LEDGER_PATH ?? 'sakk-ledger.json'` (cwd-relative); src/guard-install.mjs:31-32 the installed command is `node sakk.mjs hook --agent <agent>` with no ledger path; bin/sakk.mjs calls writeConfig only from cap off / cap set, so config.ledgerPath is never written by any command.

SAKK_LEDGER_PATH, both unset) — and nothing (not init, not guard install, no dedicated command) binds the two together, so the stop the operator writes lands where the hook never looks.
why: The kill switch was built as two pieces — a CLI that writes a halt record to a ledger, and a hook that reads halt from a ledger — each given its own path-resolution rule, on the assumption that the operator would point both at the same file.

guard install writes the hook command with no ledger path and no SAKK_LEDGER_PATH, and no CLI command writes config.ledgerPath, so the only thing that can connect the two is an environment variable the operator must remember to export (or a hand-edited config.json) — a required step with no command and no default.

The halt was only ever tested with the ledger path supplied explicitly (the happy path); the default-install round-trip — does a stop written by the CLI actually reach a freshly installed hook? — was never exercised, so the silently-inert default never surfaced.
findings.root_cause: The kill-switch ledger is one thing addressed by two divergent resolution rules (CLI cwd-default vs hook config/env lookup) with no mechanism binding them, so out of the box the operator's halt and the hook's halt-lookup name different files; the control is inert by default and fails silently rather than refusing to arm.
