findings.title: The secret guard matches the literal argv token against the secret-name regex, so a shell expansion that resolves to the secret at run time — a glob (cat .e*), a brace (cat .e{nv,xample}) or a variable (f=.env; cat $f) — is classified as a read of a harmless name and allowed, while the same file read by its spelled-out name is denied
findings.symptom: Over the installed PreToolUse hook, `cat .env` is denied (reason names protect-secret-files / secret.read) but `cat .e*`, `cat .en?`, `cat .??*`, `cat .e{nv,xample}` and `f=.env; cat $f` are all ALLOWED, even though the shell expands each to .env before cat runs. `cat "$HOME/.env"` is denied too — but only incidentally, because the literal token ends in the path segment `.env` that the pattern match catches, NOT because $HOME is resolved (the deny reason prints the unexpanded string `$HOME/.env`). The guard performs no shell expansion of any kind, so any form whose spelled-out token does not already contain the secret name as a path segment reads the very file the guard exists to protect.
findings.evidence: test test/secret-guard.test.mjs 'GAP K-SEC-043/K-SEC-045 ...' drives normalize+evaluate (the SHIPPED hook, src/hook.mjs) in a mkdtemp HOME/SAKK_HOME/cwd: Bash events `cat .env`, `cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa`, `cat "$HOME/.env"` all return verdict deny with a reason matching /protect-secret-files/ (the deny for `$HOME/.env` prints the literal `$HOME/.env`, confirming no expansion happened — it matched the trailing `.env`); Bash events `cat .e*`, `cat .en?`, `cat .??*`, `cat .e{nv,xample}`, `f=.env; cat $f` each return verdict allow with an empty reason (no secret deny). src/classify.mjs shellActions() emits {action:'file.read', path:<literal token>} and src/hook.mjs isSecretPath() matches the literal token against the SECRET name pattern, so `.e*` / `.e{nv,xample}` / `$f` never match while `$HOME/.env` and `.ssh/id_rsa` do, purely by the spelling of the written token.
findings.direct_cause: shellActions classifies each command word as a literal path and isSecretPath matches it against a fixed secret-name pattern; the shell performs pathname (glob), brace and variable expansion AFTER the hook has classified the pre-expansion word, and the classifier resolves none of it, so a token whose written spelling does not contain the secret name (`.e*`, `.e{nv,xample}`, `$f`) is allowed even though it expands to the secret before cat opens it.
why: The secret guard was built to recognise a protected file by its NAME, and name-matching was implemented against the argv token as written, on the unstated assumption that the token the agent types is the path the reader opens.

The shell sits between the classified command and the file system and rewrites the token (glob, brace, variable, command substitution) before the reader runs; the classifier performs no expansion at all — it matches the written token against the secret pattern — so a path like "$HOME/.env" is caught only incidentally (its spelled-out tail is `.env`), while any expansion form that does not already contain the secret name produces a token that cannot match.

The secret-read tests exercised spelled-out readers and paths (cat/grep/cp .env, ~/.ssh/...); none fed a command whose protected target only appears after shell expansion, so the gap between the inspected name and the opened name was never exercised and never surfaced.
findings.root_cause: The protected file is one thing addressed by two names — the pre-expansion argv token the guard inspects and the post-expansion path the OS opens — and the classifier binds its decision to the first while the read happens on the second; absent a rule that treats any word which could expand to a secret as a secret read (or that refuses to classify what it cannot safely expand), the guard protects only the spellings it happens to recognise.
findings.sweep: Swept 2026-10-28 over the shipped hook (normalize+evaluate) with HOME outside the project. Readers: cat/head with ./, ../, quotes and a backslash are denied; $(…) and bash -c "cat .env" are denied (the inner literal is parsed); backticks, eval, bash -c "$X", source, python -c and node -e are asked (shell.constructed); glob, brace and variable reads (cat .e*, .en?, .??*, .e{nv,x}, f=.env; cat $f, cat "$F", sh -c "cat .e*", cp .e* /tmp/x) and readers that pick the file themselves (grep -r, find -exec cat, xargs cat) are allowed — the boundary decision D5 keeps and the README now states. Symmetric write/delete/exec case: a glob outside the project is still refused or asked, because its literal prefix is outside (rm ~/.sak*/config.json deny, echo x > ~/.sa*/config.json ask, mv ~/.sa*/… deny); a target or flag held in a variable is allowed wherever it points (f=~/.sakk/config.json; rm $f, … echo {} > $f, d=~; rm -rf $d, o=--force; git push $o, git push --for{ce,}) — a different surface whose fix is a separate product decision, filed as F-176.

findings.title: On a Claude Code too old to honor onFailure, `sakk guard install claude-code` writes a hook that fails OPEN and tells the operator nothing: the install prints success, the onFailure line is simply omitted, and neither the CLI output nor `sakk doctor` warns that a hook which fails to run will let the call through
findings.symptom: On old Claude Code (claude --version absent or < 2.1.295), install writes the hook without onFailure:'block' — correct, since the old binary would choke on the unknown key — but the only signal is the ABSENCE of the trailing clause in the success line. The operator sees `claude-code: guard added to <path>` and `next: sakk doctor`, runs doctor, and sees nothing flagging that their guard is fail-open: if the hook process ever fails to start (bad node path, syntax error, OOM), the agent's action proceeds unguarded. A control whose whole purpose is to fail closed is silently installed fail-open.
findings.evidence: test test/guard.test.mjs 'GAP G-INS-006 ...' calls install('claude-code', {cwd, home, supportsOnFailure:false}) and asserts the returned onFailure is false and the written settings carry no onFailure key (fail-open on old CC) — AND that nothing surfaces it: the operator-facing path is exercised via the real CLI (spawnSync bin/sakk.mjs guard install claude-code) in an isolated HOME/cwd whose `claude` shim reports an old version, and stdout contains no warning (no /fail open/i, /fails? open/i). src/guard-install.mjs claudeSupportsOnFailure() returns false when `claude --version` throws or is < 2.1.295; withGuard adds onFailure only when truthy; bin/sakk.mjs:599 appends the reassuring 'a hook that fails to run blocks the call' clause ONLY when r.onFailure is truthy, and prints nothing in its place when false; doctor() returns no check for this condition.
findings.direct_cause: The fail-open branch is reached by OMISSION — withGuard leaves onFailure off and the CLI leaves its success-line clause off — so the degraded state is encoded as the absence of text rather than as an explicit warning, and no doctor check turns that absence into a visible, actionable finding.
why: Supporting old Claude Code required install to DROP onFailure rather than emit a key the old binary rejects; the drop was implemented as a silent conditional (add the clause when supported, add nothing when not), so the safe-for-old-CC path and the warn-the-operator path were conflated into one branch that does neither.

The success line was written to describe the good case ('a hook that fails to run blocks the call') and simply suppressed in the degraded case, on the assumption that an operator would notice the missing clause — but a missing sentence is not a signal, and the operator has no baseline to compare against.

doctor was built to check that the hook FIRES (its wiring and that the binary is reachable); it was never given a check for the fail-open-by-fallback condition, so the one tool the CLI points the operator at ('next: sakk doctor') is silent on exactly the risk the fallback introduces.
findings.root_cause: A degraded, less-safe install is treated as a success with a shorter message instead of a success with a warning: the loss of fail-closed behavior on old Claude Code is represented by absent output at both surfaces (CLI line and doctor) rather than by an explicit, testable warning, so absence of the guarantee is read as presence of a normal install.
findings.sweep: Swept: the onFailure degrade applies only to claude-code — cursor and codex hooks are written with failClosed:true unconditionally in withGuard, so there is no sibling guarantee that could be silently dropped. doctor's other reports already use pass/warn/fail (node, policy, decision log, start-folder, cursor double run), so no other present-or-absent guarantee was found reported as a bare success line.
findings.mechanism_gap: The install/packaging detectors assert the install round-trips and that the SHIPPED plugin manifest carries onFailure:'block' (test/release.test.mjs), and guard.test.mjs asserts withGuard sets onFailure when told to; none drives the old-Claude-Code path (supportsOnFailure:false) and asserts the operator is WARNED that the resulting hook is fail-open, so a success-shaped install that silently drops the fail-closed guarantee was outside every existing detector.

findings.title: A `sakk prices update` / `sakk prices add` command is named across docs, specs and two runtime hint strings the CLI prints to operators, but was never implemented — `prices` routes to a read-only lister, so an operator hitting PRICE_UNKNOWN is told to run a command that errors, and F-161's release detector stays green because its regex validates only a command's first token
findings.symptom: Docs (docs/SPEND.md), specs (specs/spend/{spec,contract,decide}.md) and — the live-harm surfaces — two runtime strings the CLI prints to operators tell them to run `sakk prices update` (and `sakk prices add <model>`) to refresh or extend the price table. Neither subcommand exists: bin/sakk.mjs routes `prices` to a read-only lister only. src/spend.mjs's PRICE_UNKNOWN hint reads '... run sakk prices update, or add the model to <home>/prices.json' and src/console.mjs's approximate-cost note reads 'Approximate - run sakk prices update.', so an operator who hits an unpriced model is told by the CLI's own output to run a command that returns a usage error. The only real refresh paths are re-running scripts/prices-trim.mjs (maintainers) and writing a sakk-prices.v1 table at SAKK_HOME/prices.json (operators).
findings.evidence: grep for `prices update`/`prices add` across the package finds CHANGELOG.md, specs/spend/spec.md, specs/spend/contract.md, specs/spend/decide.md, docs/SPEND.md, findings/acks/oss-m2-spend.json, src/spend.mjs (the PRICE_UNKNOWN hint string) and src/console.mjs (the approximate-cost note string). bin/sakk.mjs's command table routes `prices` to a read-only lister with no `update`/`add` case. test/release.test.mjs 'every command the README shows is a real sakk subcommand' stays GREEN because its regex /\bsakk ([a-z][a-z-]+)/ captures only the first token, so `sakk prices update` is validated as `prices` (a real subcommand); it also scans only README/CHANGELOG code spans, never runtime src/*.mjs strings or specs/.
findings.direct_cause: A command that was documented and emitted in runtime hints was never wired into bin/sakk.mjs, and the one honesty detector that could catch it (F-161's) cannot see it: its regex captures only a command's first token, so a multi-word phantom passes as its real first word, and it scans only README/CHANGELOG code spans, not the runtime hint strings or the specs/ where this phantom also lives.
why: The price table was designed with a refresh/extend UX (`sakk prices update` / `sakk prices add`) that was written into the specs, the CHANGELOG, docs/SPEND.md and two runtime hint strings, but the subcommands were never added to bin/sakk.mjs, which routes `prices` to a read-only lister only.

F-161 caught and fixed one instance of this phantom (the M2 CHANGELOG line) and added a release detector, but the detector validates only the first token of a documented command and scans only README/CHANGELOG code spans, and F-161's sweep was scoped to those two files ('the same overclaim cannot recur in either') — so the same phantom in the command's later tokens, in the runtime strings an operator actually reads, in docs/SPEND.md and in specs/ stayed invisible and the branch stayed green.

No detector resolves a command string that the docs or the running CLI emit against the actual subcommand table in bin/sakk.mjs, so a reference to a non-existent command is an unexercised honesty gap until an operator runs it and gets a usage error.
findings.root_cause: A user-facing command (`sakk prices update` / `add`) is named across docs, specs and two runtime hint strings but was never implemented, and the honesty detector that should catch it validates only a command's first token on two doc surfaces (README/CHANGELOG) — so a multi-word phantom on the runtime, docs and spec surfaces ships unchecked, and the running CLI tells operators to invoke a command that does not exist.
findings.sweep: Swept the phantom's whole footprint (grep `prices update`/`prices add`): CHANGELOG.md, specs/spend/{spec,contract,decide}.md, docs/SPEND.md, findings/acks/oss-m2-spend.json, and the two runtime strings src/spend.mjs (PRICE_UNKNOWN hint) and src/console.mjs (approximate-cost note). The real refresh paths that already exist are `sakk prices [--json]` (read-only view), re-running scripts/prices-trim.mjs (maintainers) and dropping a sakk-prices.v1 table at SAKK_HOME/prices.json (operators). Resolution is the same owner product decision F-161 already routed (wire the spend/cap/prices CLI vs keep `prices` read-only); until it is made, no surface is edited, so retracting references is not pre-judged against a possible decision to implement the command.
findings.mechanism_gap: The RC-10 claims-are-checked detectors resolve backticked file names and error codes in the docs against the code (test/claims-are-checked.test.mjs), and test/release.test.mjs 'every command the README shows is a real sakk subcommand' scans README/CHANGELOG code spans with a first-token-only regex (/\bsakk ([a-z][a-z-]+)/), so a multi-word command validates on its first word alone and `sakk prices update` passes as `prices`; no detector scans runtime src/*.mjs strings or specs/ for a command reference. The phantom sits in exactly the surfaces and the token position F-161's detector left uncovered.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: whether to retract the `sakk prices update`/`add` references (docs, specs, and the two runtime hint strings) or to implement them as real subcommands is the owner product decision F-161 already routed; widening the release detector to validate every token of a multi-word command and to scan runtime src/*.mjs command strings is deferred until that decision, so the detector does not go red against text that may be about to become true.

findings.title: A delete, write or flag held in a shell variable is judged by the bare `$name`, so `f=~/.sakk/config.json; rm $f`, `d=~; rm -rf $d` and `o=--force; git push $o` are allowed while the same command written out is denied — the agent can remove its own cap and the guard state the D4 confirmation rests on
findings.symptom: Over the installed hook (bin/sakk.mjs hook, HOME outside the project), `rm ~/.sakk/config.json`, `echo {} > ~/.sakk/config.json`, `rm -rf ~` and `git push --force origin main` are each denied, but `f=~/.sakk/config.json; rm $f`, `f=~/.sakk/config.json; echo {} > $f`, `d=~; rm -rf $d`, `o=--force; git push $o origin main` and `git push --for{ce,} origin main` are each allowed with no reason. The README's cap paragraph promised that the agent cannot silently raise its own cap; with a variable it can delete or blank the config that holds the cap.
findings.evidence: test test/guard.test.mjs 'a guard-state, outside-repo or destructive-git target held in a shell variable or brace is asked, never allowed (F-176)' runs the real CLI hook (spawnSync bin/sakk.mjs hook --agent claude-code) in a mkdtemp world with HOME and the repo apart: the written-out forms return deny; a glob outside the project (`rm ~/.sak*/config.json`) is not allowed; before the fix the five variable/brace forms returned allow (empty stdout — red baseline re-run 2026-10-29), after it they return ask, and a deny beside an expansion still wins. Found while running the F-173 sweep for the symmetric write/delete/exec case (probe over normalize+evaluate, 2026-10-28); D11 (2026-10-29) decided ask, never allow.
findings.direct_cause: shellActions takes each argument and redirect target as a literal path or flag; `$f` is resolved against the cwd as a relative name inside the project and `$o` / `--for{ce,}` match no destructive flag, so protect-guard-state, deny-rm-outside-repo, deny-delete-protected and shell-destructive never see the target the shell substitutes before the command runs.
why: The guard's write, delete and destructive-git rules were built to recognise a protected target by the path or flag written in the command, on the assumption that the word the agent types is the word the command receives.

The shell substitutes variables (and expands braces) after the hook has classified the word; the classifier resolves none of it and treats an unresolved word as an ordinary relative path or argument, which names nothing protected — so the decision falls through to allow instead of to ask.

The guard-state and destructive-command tests drove only written-out targets, and the one test of run-time-built commands (shell.constructed) covers a variable in command position (`bash -c "$X"`), not in argument position; no detector fed a protected target through a variable, so the gap between the judged word and the used word was never exercised.
findings.root_cause: An unresolved shell word is classified as if it were the literal it spells, so the protected target is addressed by two names — the `$name` the guard judges and the path the shell substitutes — and absent a rule that a word the guard cannot resolve is asked rather than allowed, every protection keyed on a target's name stops at the spellings it recognises.
findings.sweep: Swept per D11 (ask, never allow): the expansion flag is raised in shellSegments, the single tokenizer every target-keyed rule reads, so protect-guard-state, protect-guard-state-delete, deny-rm-outside-repo, deny-delete-protected, shell-destructive, ask-write-outside and the deploy rules all inherit it — a variable or brace expansion in any argument, redirect target, flag, double-quoted word or wrapped (sudo/env) command makes the command shell.constructed. Sibling paths exercised in the detector: redirect targets, flags, word-start braces, double quotes, sh -c recursion; the non-expanding look-alikes stay unflagged (single-quoted and backslash-escaped text, the find placeholder, fd redirects, a trailing dollar sign). Deny still outranks the new ask (worst-wins), asserted in the detector; the F-173 run-time-pick boundary (glob, recursive grep, find -exec, xargs) is deliberately kept allowed and re-pinned in test/secret-guard.test.mjs. no follow-up needed: every target-keyed rule reads the same tokenizer flag.
findings.instance_fix: this commit

findings.mechanism_gap: The guard-state and destructive-command detectors (test/guard.test.mjs 'the agent cannot write the policy it is judged by', the shell-destructive cases, test/spend.test.mjs 'the agent cannot raise its own cap…') assert denies on written-out targets only; none drives a protected target or flag through a shell variable or brace, so a word the classifier cannot resolve but the shell substitutes was outside every existing guard detector.

findings.title: An agent the guard binds can lift another agent's halt, clear the books or break the ledger lock (`sakk resume|reconcile|unlock --by <any name>`), and can write the default in-repo ledger directly — the hook judges neither as the ledger write it is
findings.symptom: A per-agent halt, a reconciliation hold and the ledger lock are meant to wait for a person. resume, reconcile and unlock ask for --by <name>, but the name is self-declared (README limits), and the hook classifies `sakk resume --by alice --agent bot-7`, `sakk reconcile --by alice` and `sakk unlock --by alice` as a plain shell.run, so an agent that is not itself halted gets them allowed. The default ledger is sakk-ledger.json in the working folder, an in-repo file the shipped policy lets the agent write. A global halt still holds, because it denies every call but reading.
findings.evidence: test: test/kill-switch.test.mjs 'GAP F-177 the hook lets an agent run the commands that lift a halt or clear the books' feeds the three commands through the real hook evaluate() in an isolated HOME/SAKK_HOME/project and asserts each is allowed. bin/sakk.mjs ledgerPath() falls back to ledgerFrom('sakk-ledger.json') in the current directory, and policies/guard-default.json protects only .sakk/ and ~sakk/ from file.write.
findings.direct_cause: src/classify.mjs maps a sakk command to the write it makes only for cap and guard (F-171); resume, reconcile and unlock fall through to shell.run, and the ledger file is not named by any guard-state scope, so neither the command nor a direct edit of the ledger reaches protect-guard-state.
why: F-171 was scoped to the controls the D4 product decision named (cap and guard), and the halt family was assumed covered because it already demanded --by, though that name only attributes and never authorizes.

The ledger was designed as the library's spend book for an orchestrator, so its default home is the working folder; when the hook began reading halts from it, it became guard state without moving out of the agent's reach.
No test drove the halt-family commands from a second, non-halted agent, so the cross-agent lift never surfaced.
findings.root_cause: The hook judges the agent by what a command says, and only cap and guard are taught to say the guard-state write the sakk binary makes; the ledger that holds halts is guard state in meaning but not in scope, so an agent can lift a halt either by running sakk or by editing the file.
findings.sweep: Not swept — the fix needs a decision: whether the hook denies resume, reconcile and unlock from an agent (as it now denies cap), and whether the ledger moves under ~/.sakk or gets its own guard-state scope in the shipped policy. Once decided, sweep every path that writes the ledger (CLI, MCP gate, console) for the same agent reach.
findings.mechanism_gap: The F-171 detectors (J-UAT-016) assert the hook's judgment of cap and guard commands and the CLI's terminal gate; nothing asserts the hook's judgment of the halt-family commands, or that the file holding halts is in a scope the agent may not write, so a control lifted through the ledger was outside every check.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/kill-switch.test.mjs::GAP F-177 the hook lets an agent run the commands that lift a halt or clear the books

distinct_from.F-49: F-49 is a concurrency lost-update: a human-forced unlock during a halt lets a racing reserve overwrite the halt write. F-177 has no race: a second agent runs resume, reconcile or unlock under any name, or edits the in-repo ledger, and the hook allows it. Different axis — mutual-exclusion loss vs the agent reaching the ledger that holds its own controls.

findings.title: The guard-resolution check demanded that a guard a revision had superseded still resolve, so a gap test could not be renamed to its fix
findings.symptom: Closing J-UAT-016 (F-171) renamed the gap test 'GAP J-UAT-016 agent-issued cap off / cap set / guard uninstall are currently allowed' to the fix's name and appended a C-11.1 revision naming the new test — the R2 path for a correction. findings-check --staged then refused the commit: the committed top-level C-11.1 guard no longer resolved, and R2 forbids rewriting it. The only ways through were a test or comment that keeps the stale gap name alive, or a rewrite of a committed answer.
findings.evidence: node scripts/findings-check.mjs --staged on oss/p0-uat-backfill, 2026-10-28: 'C-11.1: guard test/kill-switch.test.mjs::GAP J-UAT-016 agent-issued cap off / cap set / guard uninstall are currently allowed does not resolve (no such file or name)'. scripts/findings-lib.mjs guardResolution checked the top-level guard and every revision's guard alike.
findings.direct_cause: guardResolution required every guard an answer had ever named to resolve, while ackRewrites freezes the committed guard; a revision could add a new guard but never retire the old one.
why: The resolution rule was written and tested from the side it must catch — a guard naming a test that does not exist yet — and never against a guard legitimately superseded.
Before F-171 no gap-pinned guard had been closed, so the revision path had only carried corrected answers whose old guards still existed.
The ledger already records a renamed check as a correction (mechanism_upgrade from the old value), but the answers check did not read the ledger.
findings.root_cause: A detector tuned on one side: guard resolution was measured only on missing guards, so the documented correction path for a closed gap was refused as if it were a stale reference.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: a guard a later revision supersedes is exempt from resolution only when that revision's finding carries a correction whose from is exactly the old guard with a 20-character why; the current guard always resolves, and a missing or malformed ledger retires nothing
findings.guard: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::a guard a revision supersedes may stop resolving only when the revision's finding records the rename (F-178)
findings.sweep: The other answers-file rules re-read for the same one-sided tuning: ackRewrites (R2) is tested on rewrites and on the legitimate revision path; missingAnswers on missing, short, copied and benign answers (F-119); guardProblem's shape rule on test and non-test paths. Only resolution lacked the legitimate side. Five mutants of the new rule (no retirement, any finding retires, the current guard retirable, any correction retires, no why length) each turn the tests red.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-13 detectors (F-119's benign corpus of real answers) cover the answer-text rules; guard resolution was a separate detector whose tests held only failing references, so the first legitimate supersede was outside them.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/self-evolution.test.mjs::a guard a revision supersedes may stop resolving only when the revision's finding records the rename (F-178)

findings.title: The cache_creation split can still lower the bill: parseLine reads a malformed split field as 0, and costOf honours a split that names only part of the cache writes
findings.symptom: With cache_creation_input_tokens:1000 the right charge is about $0.00393 (test price table). A split of {5m:-1, 1h:100} was billed $0.00078 and a split of {5m:400} $0.00168: the split replaced the aggregate even though it named fewer tokens. A split field of "1000", 1000.5 or true was silently read as 0 rather than marked unreadable; with the aggregate present that happened to fall back to it, but a row carrying only the split lost those writes entirely. The daily cap counts less than was spent.
findings.evidence: probe on oss/p0-uat-backfill at fe936ca: costOf(entry, parseLine(line).call.usage) for aggregate 1000 and each split above; parseLine({cache_creation:{ephemeral_5m_input_tokens:'1000'}}) returned a call with ephemeral_5m_input_tokens 0. src/spend.mjs parseLine screened only the four top-level counts (USAGE_FIELDS) and coerced split fields with `tokenCount(x) ? x : 0`; src/prices.mjs costOf replaced the aggregate whenever s5 + s1h > 0.
findings.direct_cause: parseLine applied the F-170 whole-token screen to the four top-level counts and a coerce-to-zero to the two split fields, and costOf, after F-168, trusted any split that named at least one token as the complete breakdown.
why: F-168 fixed the case it was found on (an empty split) by special-casing zero, not the rule the case broke: a breakdown refines the price of the aggregate and never shrinks it.
F-170 screened the counts in USAGE_FIELDS, a hand-written list of top-level fields, so the nested split fields stayed on the older coerce-to-zero path written before the screen existed.

The spec's input-space table lists 'negative / NaN / strings (→ unreadable)' for usage without naming which fields, and no test walked every numeric field, so the table's claim went unchecked for the two nested ones.
findings.root_cause: Both earlier fixes covered the instances they were found on (the empty split, the top-level counts) instead of the rule those instances share, so the next instance of each rule passed: a partial split, and a malformed nested count.
findings.instance_fix: this commit: parseLine marks a cache_creation that is not an object, or a split field that is present, not null and not a whole-token count, unreadable (the cap then fails closed, SPEND_UNREADABLE); costOf bills the 1-hour split at its price and max(5-minute split, aggregate minus 1-hour split) at the 5-minute price, so a split refines the aggregate and never lowers it, and split tokens count toward the long-context threshold. specs/spend/spec.md states both rules.
findings.class_fix: test/spend.test.mjs::every numeric field of a real usage line is either priced or declared unpriced
findings.guard: test/spend.test.mjs::a cache split never prices below the same usage without it
findings.sweep: Every numeric field of a real Claude Code usage block is now enumerated: the four counts and two split fields are priced and each is driven through seven malformed values at parse and six at pricing; the server_tool_use request counts are the only unpriced numeric fields and are filed as F-180. mergeCall takes the maximum of each field and feeds costOf, which now never shrinks the aggregate, so a merge of partial observations cannot lower the bill. Six mutants of the fix (no split screen, no object check, arrays allowed, the old >0 rule, the split alone, the old long-context prompt) each turn the suite red.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-02 detectors enumerate from the source for directories, keys, codes and env variables; none enumerates the fields of a parsed usage record, so the F-170 screen over a hand-written field list and the F-168 zero special-case both passed every check while the spec's input-space table claimed the whole usage space.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/spend.test.mjs::every numeric field of a real usage line is either priced or declared unpriced

distinct_from.F-168: F-168 was the empty split priced at zero; F-179 is the rule that fix did not state: a split naming some but not all writes still undercounted, and a malformed split field read as 0.
distinct_from.F-170: F-170 was a fractional top-level count crashing pricing unisolated; F-179 is the nested split fields that screen never reached, which were coerced to 0 rather than crashing.

findings.title: The daily spend cap prices tokens only; per-request server-tool charges a usage block reports (server_tool_use web searches) are left out, and no document says so
findings.symptom: A day whose calls run web searches is reported and capped lower than it was billed: the API bills each server-side web search per request on top of the tokens, and sakk spend counts the tokens alone. A user who sets a $5 cap reads it as $5 of model spend.
findings.evidence: test/spend.test.mjs 'every numeric field of a real usage line is either priced or declared unpriced' walks a Claude Code usage block: server_tool_use.web_search_requests and server_tool_use.web_fetch_requests are its only numeric fields that neither parseLine keeps nor costOf prices. specs/spend/spec.md Price defines cost as the sum over token kinds; README and docs/SPEND.md describe a daily dollar cap without the limit.
findings.direct_cause: The price model and the snapshot were built around token kinds; request-priced server tools were not in the model, and the cap's documentation did not declare the omission.
why: The spend design took LiteLLM's token prices as the whole cost of a call, and the per-request search price lives in a separate field of the same table that was never read.
The input-space table enumerated token fields only, so a numeric usage field that is not a token count had no row.
No test listed every numeric field a real usage block carries, so the unpriced one was invisible until the F-179 enumeration listed them.
findings.root_cause: A cost the cap cannot see is absent from the reading, and the absence reads as zero spend instead of being declared as a limit.
findings.sweep: Not swept — pricing server tools is a product decision for the owner (a request-price field in the table and the snapshot, or a declared limit). This branch declares the limit in specs/spend/spec.md and docs/SPEND.md; the enumeration test names the two unpriced fields, so a decision either way is one edit there.
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-01 detectors catch an absent key, flag or file turning into a pass in the CLI, bundles and CI; a cost kind missing from the price model is absence in the data model, outside every one of them.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/spend.test.mjs::every numeric field of a real usage line is either priced or declared unpriced

distinct_from.F-168: F-168 was a token kind the model prices (cache writes) dropped by an empty breakdown; F-180 is a charge the model has no kind for at all (per-request server tools), so it is missing from every row, not misread in one.
distinct_from.F-170: F-170 was a malformed token count crashing pricing; F-180 is well-formed usage whose request counts are outside the price model, read without error and simply not priced.

findings.title: An agent can run sakk init and re-point the ledger the hook reads halts from, so a halt held on another ledger stops applying; the F-171 fix denied cap and guard by name, not every subcommand that loosens a control
findings.symptom: A person halts one agent on the ledger SAKK_LEDGER_PATH names. A second, un-halted agent runs 'sakk init --cap 5 --ledger ./x.json'; the hook allows it as an in-repo shell command, init records the agent's in-repo ledger in ~/.sakk/config.json, the hook reads that ledger first, and the halted agent's next destructive call is allowed.
findings.evidence: test/kill-switch.test.mjs 'J-UAT-016 an agent cannot re-point the ledger a halt is read from (F-181)': before this commit the hook answered allow (allow-in-repo) for the init command, and after the CLI ran it the cursor agent halted on the ops ledger had 'rm -rf build' allowed. F-171's sweep text: 'init, scan --install-hook and guard install only tighten ... and never replace a recorded one'.
findings.direct_cause: classify.mjs judged sakk cap as the config.json write and sakk guard as the agent-config write, and every other sakk subcommand as shell.run, so init, which writes config.json too, fell through to allow-in-repo.
why: The F-171 fix named the two subcommands its finding showed (cap, guard) instead of stating the rule that every Sakk command is judged by the write it makes.

F-171's sweep judged init as tightening because it never replaces a recorded ledgerPath, and missed the case where none is recorded and the hook found the ledger through SAKK_LEDGER_PATH: recording one then moves the hook off it.
The F-172 change that made the hook read config.ledgerPath first turned init into a loosening command, and nothing re-judged the subcommands when a control's source changed.
No test enumerated the CLI's subcommands, so a subcommand's effect on a control was decided once in prose and never checked again.
findings.root_cause: A list of the commands a finding showed stood in for the rule that every command which can loosen a control is judged as the write it makes, and the list was not tied to the CLI's own dispatch table, so a command whose effect changed later stayed off it.

findings.title: The 10-27 P0 acceptance counted a case as passed when a test with a matching name existed, not when the case's expected outcome was observed
findings.symptom: The 10-27 acceptance report marked 20 of the 37 cases that fail on 10-28 as pass or 'covered by tests'. Run black-box against each case's own expectation, they fail. Some matched tests pin the current behaviour (test/release.test.mjs:177 asserts init's present output, not a working guard); others use narrower input than the case (test/console.test.mjs:763-780 checks redaction with a command field only).
findings.evidence: P0 black-box UAT 2026-10-28 at 8edbc8e, run through the sandboxed runner with a throwaway HOME (findings/reviews/2026-10-28-p0-uat-blackbox.md): of 151 P0 cases, 102 pass, 37 fail, 5 known-open, 5 manual, 2 documented limits. 20 of the 37 failures were reported pass or covered on 10-27; the other 17 were already deferred to V2 on 10-27. The review's per-case table puts the 10-27 verdict next to the 10-28 one.
findings.direct_cause: The 10-27 acceptance joined each case to tests by name and keyword and took a found test as the verdict, without running the case's steps against its expected outcome.
why: A matching test name shows the area has a test, not that the test asserts what the case expects; several matched tests pin today's behaviour or use narrower input than the case.
The acceptance report format accepted 'covered by test X' as a verdict, so no observation per case was required.
The weak-evidence checks (C-06) were built for eval reports and evidence bundles, not for the acceptance report written for the owner.
findings.root_cause: Acceptance evidence was defined as 'a related test exists' instead of 'the case's expected outcome was observed', and no check on the acceptance report required an observation per case.
findings.sweep: Not swept — deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28). docs/V2-BACKLOG.md lists the fix and the sweep: every acceptance verdict cites an observed run (command, exit code, output) of the case's own steps. Done once on 10-28 for all 151 P0 cases; the rule goes into the acceptance template for V2.
findings.mechanism_gap: The weak-evidence detectors (eval case packs FAKE→HARNESS_ONLY, evidence-bundle METRICS_UNVERIFIABLE) check eval reports and bundles; an acceptance verdict is outside their input, so a verdict backed only by a test-name match reached the owner with no observation behind it.

findings.title: Command names and protected folders are compared case-sensitively, while the default macOS volume resolves names case-insensitively
findings.symptom: On a case-insensitive APFS volume, an upper- or mixed-case spelling of a destructive command's name, or of a protected folder (guard state, agent config, CI workflows), runs the same program or reaches the same file. The guard's rules match only the lower-case spelling and allow it.
findings.evidence: P0 black-box UAT 2026-10-28 at 8edbc8e, run through the sandboxed runner with a throwaway HOME (findings/reviews/2026-10-28-p0-uat-blackbox.md): cases G-SEC-003/004 (case variants of the delete and git command names: allow) and G-SEC-006/007/008 (case variants of the guard-state, agent-config and CI-workflow folders: allow, while the lower-case forms deny or ask). Inbox items d24d35 and ded5a4.
findings.direct_cause: The classifier compares a command's program name, and the matcher compares canonical paths, byte for byte. Neither folds case, and the canonical-path step resolves symlinks and '..' but not the volume's case-insensitive lookup.
why: The rules assume one spelling names one program or file. That holds on Linux, not on the default macOS and Windows volumes.
The guard tests drive each protected name with the spelling the rule lists; no test drives a case variant.
Folding case changes what every scope rule matches, so the change waits on the owner; D10 deferred it to V2.
findings.root_cause: The guard names a protected program or file by its exact bytes, while the operating system finds both through a case-insensitive lookup on the default volumes — two names for one target.
findings.sweep: Not swept — deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28). docs/V2-BACKLOG.md lists the fix and the sweep: fold case (or ask on a case variant) for program names and every scope rule when the volume is case-insensitive; drive each protected-name rule with a case variant.
findings.mechanism_gap: The two-names detectors (ledger.test F-85 symlinked ledger file, stranger-regressions relative --out, guard.test 'a delete that takes the repository, the home folder or Sakk state…') cover links and relative forms; none spells a protected program or folder in another case, so a case variant was outside their inputs.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28); docs/V2-BACKLOG.md names the detector to add

distinct_from.F-184: F-184 is git option parsing (clustered, abbreviated, aliased flags); F-183 is case folding of names on a case-insensitive volume.
distinct_from.F-186: F-186 is a symlink with an unrelated name pointing at a secret file; F-183 is the same name in another case.

findings.title: A git force push is recognised only in its written-out flag forms; other spellings git accepts for the same flag pass
findings.symptom: git accepts its force flag inside a cluster of short options, as an unambiguous prefix of the long option, and through an alias defined inline for one command. The guard's destructive-git rule recognises the separate short and the full long spelling only, and allows the other forms.
findings.evidence: P0 black-box UAT 2026-10-28 at 8edbc8e, run through the sandboxed runner with a throwaway HOME (findings/reviews/2026-10-28-p0-uat-blackbox.md): cases G-SEC-005 and J-UAT-015: the clustered, abbreviated and inline-alias forms return allow; the separate flag forms deny. Inbox item 9b254d.
findings.direct_cause: The git classifier matches flag tokens against a fixed list of spellings instead of parsing options the way git does (short-option clusters, unique long-option prefixes, inline alias definitions).
why: The rule lists the spellings the git docs show; git's option parser accepts more forms for the same flag.
The destructive-git tests use the listed spellings only, so only the positive path was driven.
An inline alias moves the force flag out of the command's own words, which a token list cannot see.
findings.root_cause: One git option has several spellings git treats as the same flag, and the guard recognises it by a partial list of them.
findings.sweep: Not swept — deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28). docs/V2-BACKLOG.md lists the fix and the sweep: parse git options as git does (clusters, unique long prefixes) and ask on any inline alias definition; check every flag-keyed git and shell rule for the same forms.
findings.mechanism_gap: The destructive-command detectors (guard.test 'every wrapper, with a flag that takes a value, still names the command', the delete-that-takes cases) feed each flag in its listed spellings; none generates the other forms git's parser accepts.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28); docs/V2-BACKLOG.md names the detector to add

distinct_from.F-176: F-176 is a destructive target or flag held in a variable; F-184 is the force flag written directly in a form git's option parser accepts but the rule's list omits (clusters, prefixes, an inline alias).
distinct_from.F-183: F-183 is case folding of program and folder names; F-184 is git option parsing — the flag's spelling, not its case.
distinct_from.F-186: F-186 is a read through a symlink to a secret file; F-184 is a git force flag spelled in an unlisted form.

findings.title: A read through a symlink to a secret file is judged by the link's name, although the guard spec says paths are resolved through symlinks
findings.symptom: A symlink with an ordinary name that points at a .env file or an SSH private key can be read with the agent's Read tool; the guard allows it because the link's own name is not secret-shaped.
findings.evidence: P0 black-box UAT 2026-10-28 at 8edbc8e, run through the sandboxed runner with a throwaway HOME (findings/reviews/2026-10-28-p0-uat-blackbox.md): case K-SEC-044: four reads through such links return allow (empty stdout, exit 0). specs/guard/spec.md:90 says a path that cannot be made canonical after resolving symlinks, '~' and '..' refuses.
findings.direct_cause: The secret-read rule matches the path as written. The realpath step in src/classify.mjs resolves the directory part used to name the scope, not the final component the read opens.
why: Resolution was added to name a path's scope (which folder it is in), where only the directory matters.
The secret-file tests name the secret file directly; no test reads through a link with an ordinary name.
The spec states the stronger property, so a reader of the spec assumes link reads are covered.
findings.root_cause: One file has two names — the link and its target — and the secret rule judges the link's name while the read reaches the target.
findings.sweep: Not swept — deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28). docs/V2-BACKLOG.md lists the fix and the sweep: resolve the final path component before every secret and scope rule (read, write, delete); drive each rule with a link to a protected target.
findings.mechanism_gap: The two-names detector for links (ledger.test F-85 symlinked ledger file) covers the ledger's own write path; no guard detector reads through a link to a secret file.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28); docs/V2-BACKLOG.md names the detector to add

findings.title: In a project-local install the policy in use and the hook's code sit under node_modules, which the agent may change or delete
findings.symptom: Installed into the project's node_modules, the hook runs that copy's code and reads that copy's default policy. The agent can rewrite the policy or the hook source, or delete the package folder, and the guard allows it.
findings.evidence: P0 black-box UAT 2026-10-28 at 8edbc8e, run through the sandboxed runner with a throwaway HOME (findings/reviews/2026-10-28-p0-uat-blackbox.md): case J-UAT-017: writes to the installed package's policies/guard-default.json and src/hook.mjs return allow, and a recursive delete of the package folder returns allow; the same kind of target in Sakk's state folders denies (protect-guard-state).
findings.direct_cause: The guard-state rule protects ~/.sakk, the project's .sakk/ and agent config, not the install location of the Sakk package being run.
why: The protected set was designed around a global install, where the package lives outside the project.
The install tests use a global prefix or the source tree, never a project-local node_modules.
Where the hook's code lives is decided at install time, so the protected set has to come from the install, not a fixed list.
findings.root_cause: The guard assumes it is installed outside the project it guards; in a project-local install its own code and policy are ordinary project files.
findings.sweep: Not swept — deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28). docs/V2-BACKLOG.md lists the fix and the sweep: record the installed package root at guard install and protect it like guard state, or refuse a project-local install; run the install tests in a project-local layout.
findings.mechanism_gap: The environment-assumed detectors (stranger-regressions, secret-scan 'the hook as SHIPPED') run the shipped hook from a global or source layout; none installs Sakk into the project's node_modules and tries to change it as the agent.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28); docs/V2-BACKLOG.md names the detector to add

findings.title: The requirement says the agent may not rewrite its own hook configuration; the shipped rules only ask
findings.symptom: A write to the agent's user-level settings file gets a person-approval prompt from the generic write-outside rule, and a write to the project's agent config asks (ask-agent-config). Requirement REQ-G13 expects a deny, and the user-level file is not recognised as agent config at all.
findings.evidence: P0 black-box UAT 2026-10-28 at 8edbc8e, run through the sandboxed runner with a throwaway HOME (findings/reviews/2026-10-28-p0-uat-blackbox.md): case G-SEC-011: the agent's Write and a shell redirect to the user-level settings return ask (ask-write-outside). specs/guard/spec.md:184 defines ask-agent-config as require_approval for the project-relative agent folders only.
findings.direct_cause: The guard spec chose ask for agent config and scoped it to project-relative folders, so the requirement's deny for the agent's own hook config reached neither the spec nor the policy.
why: The spec was written from its threat table (turning the guard off asks, and the doctor's fire test catches a removed hook), not line by line from the requirement.
No check maps requirement ids to spec rules, so a requirement the spec weakens raises nothing.
The user-level config is outside the project, so it falls to the generic write-outside rule.
findings.root_cause: The guard spec restates the requirement in its own words with a weaker verdict, and nothing ties the requirement's verdict to the shipped rule.
findings.sweep: Not swept — deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28). docs/V2-BACKLOG.md lists the fix and the sweep: the owner decides deny or ask for the agent's own hook config; then add the user-level agent config to the rule and map each REQ-G line to the rule and test that keep it.
findings.mechanism_gap: The statement detectors (claims-are-checked codes and file names, guard.test 'the spec lists the shipped rules in their order') tie the spec to the code; none ties the original requirement's verdicts to the spec, so a weakened verdict passes both.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28); docs/V2-BACKLOG.md names the detector to add

findings.title: sakk guard install writes a tool matcher without Grep or Glob and no permissions deny rules, so a search over secret files is never judged
findings.symptom: The matcher that sakk guard install writes for Claude Code lists Bash, PowerShell, Monitor, Read, Edit, Write, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit and mcp tools; Grep and Glob calls never reach the hook. A Grep whose glob selects .env files is allowed. The requirement's permissions deny rules (REQ-G04, reads of .env and similar) are not written. The plugin's own hook uses matcher '*' and is not affected.
findings.evidence: P0 black-box UAT 2026-10-28 at 8edbc8e, run through the sandboxed runner with a throwaway HOME (findings/reviews/2026-10-28-p0-uat-blackbox.md): cases G-SEC-012 (no Grep or Glob in the installed matcher; a Grep with an .env glob and a Glob: allow; a Grep whose path is the secret file denies only when fed to the hook directly) and G-INS-008 (install exit 0; the settings file has no permissions key).
findings.direct_cause: CLAUDE_MATCHER in src/guard-install.mjs lists the tools the classifier was written for, and install writes only the hook group, not a permissions block.
why: The matcher was built from the tools whose inputs the classifier parses; Grep and Glob read file contents but were not on that list.
The install tests assert the hook group is written, not that every file-reading tool is matched or that deny rules exist.
The permissions deny block is the requirement's second layer; the install spec dropped it with no recorded decision.
findings.root_cause: The set of tools that can read a file is listed by hand in the matcher, and the list is shorter than the tools Claude Code ships.
findings.sweep: Not swept — deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28). docs/V2-BACKLOG.md lists the fix and the sweep: match every file-reading tool and classify its path and glob inputs; write the REQ-G04 deny rules at install; test the matcher against Claude Code's tool list.
findings.mechanism_gap: The partial-list detectors (exec-env, bundle-absence, the wrapper case) check lists of wrappers and files; none compares the installed matcher with the tools that can read a file, so Grep and Glob were outside every detector's input.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28); docs/V2-BACKLOG.md names the detector to add

findings.title: A Write whose content is not a string skips the secret scan
findings.symptom: When the content of a Write is an array, object or number, the hook does not scan it for secrets and decides on the path alone, so secret-shaped content in that form is allowed.
findings.evidence: P0 black-box UAT 2026-10-28 at 8edbc8e, run through the sandboxed runner with a throwaway HOME (findings/reviews/2026-10-28-p0-uat-blackbox.md): case R-REL-001: a Write with a secret-shaped value inside non-string content returns allow; the same value as a string denies.
findings.direct_cause: src/hook.mjs scans content only when it is a string; any other type is treated as having nothing to scan.
why: Claude Code sends content as a string, so the scan was written for that shape.
Other agents and MCP clients can send structured content, and an absent string was read as 'no secret'.
The hook tests drive string content only.
findings.root_cause: The scan treats 'not a string' as 'nothing to scan', where an input it cannot read should be serialised and scanned or refused.
findings.sweep: Not swept — deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28). docs/V2-BACKLOG.md lists the fix and the sweep: scan the serialised form of non-string content, or deny it with a code; check every field the hook scans for the same type test.
findings.mechanism_gap: The absence detectors (cli-strictness 'every CLI refuses what it does not understand', bundle-absence, ci-honesty) cover CLI arguments, bundles and CI status; none feeds the hook a field of an unexpected type, so an unreadable field passed as clean.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28); docs/V2-BACKLOG.md names the detector to add

findings.title: The spend figure finds the agent's logs through the agent's own environment, so a moved log folder reads $0
findings.symptom: sakk spend and the cap check find the Claude Code logs through CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR or HOME. With either pointed at an empty folder, the day's spend reads $0 and the cap never trips. sakk cap set records no log folder, although docs/SPEND.md says the folder is fixed at cap set so an agent's environment cannot move it.
findings.evidence: P0 black-box UAT 2026-10-28 at 8edbc8e, run through the sandboxed runner with a throwaway HOME (findings/reviews/2026-10-28-p0-uat-blackbox.md): case S-SEC-010: with CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, and separately HOME, set to an empty folder, spend reads $0.00 and the hook allows; ~/.sakk/config.json after cap set has no log-folder entry.
findings.direct_cause: The log folder is resolved at read time from environment variables the agent controls; cap set writes the cap only.
why: Reading the environment matches how Claude Code finds its own folder, so it looked like the right source.
For the cap, the agent's environment is untrusted input from the party the cap binds; the docs describe the fix (record at cap set), which was not built.
The spend tests set the environment to the fixture folder, so a moved folder was never driven.
findings.root_cause: The bound party's environment decides where the guard reads the bound party's spend from.
findings.sweep: Not swept — deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28). docs/V2-BACKLOG.md lists the fix and the sweep: record the absolute log folder at cap set and read only that; ask or refuse when the environment points elsewhere; correct docs/SPEND.md in the same change (v1 states it as a limit).
findings.mechanism_gap: The untrusted-input detectors (hostile-names, mcp F-82 hostile frames) cover names and MCP frames; none treats the agent's environment variables as input to the spend reader.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28); docs/V2-BACKLOG.md names the detector to add

findings.title: One unreadable agent log makes sakk spend crash with a raw stack, and the hook's deny names the wrong cause
findings.symptom: With one log file unreadable (mode 000), sakk spend exits 1 with an uncaught EACCES stack trace, and the hook denies with 'the guard cannot read its rules', although the rules are readable and a log file is what failed.
findings.evidence: P0 black-box UAT 2026-10-28 at 8edbc8e, run through the sandboxed runner with a throwaway HOME (findings/reviews/2026-10-28-p0-uat-blackbox.md): case S-REL-001: sakk spend prints an EACCES stack from headOf (src/spend.mjs:180), exit 1; the hook denies with the rules-unreadable message.
findings.direct_cause: headOf opens each log without handling a permission error, and the hook's outer handler maps any exception to the rules-unreadable message.
why: The log reader assumes the agent's own logs are always readable by the same user.
The hook's outer handler was written for the policy load and covers every later step with the same message.
The isolation tests cover a crashing classifier and a broken policy, not a failing log read.
findings.root_cause: One failing input (a log file) is not isolated: it ends the whole spend read and is reported as another component's failure.
findings.sweep: Not swept — deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28). docs/V2-BACKLOG.md lists the fix and the sweep: isolate each log read (skip and report the unreadable file with a code; the cap fails closed under that code); give the hook a distinct code for each step that can fail.
findings.mechanism_gap: The isolation detectors (mcp F-82, scorer-rules SCORER_ERROR, self-evolution-cli) isolate a bad frame, a scorer error and a broken CLI; none makes one agent log unreadable, so its failure spread to the whole command.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28); docs/V2-BACKLOG.md names the detector to add

findings.title: An edited hot-ledger summary frees cap room; reserve trusts it, and only sakk ledger verify reports the change
findings.symptom: Lowering the settled total in the hot ledger summary (for example from $8 to $0) gives that much of the day's cap back, and reserve keeps allowing after a cold segment is lost or altered. Only an explicit sakk ledger verify reports the mismatch.
findings.evidence: P0 black-box UAT 2026-10-28 at 8edbc8e, run through the sandboxed runner with a throwaway HOME (findings/reviews/2026-10-28-p0-uat-blackbox.md): case L-REL-013: after the summary edit, the next reserve is allowed against the freed $8; after a segment is removed, reserve still allows; ledger verify reports the break.
findings.direct_cause: Reserve reads the running total from the summary without checking it against the hash chain or the index; verification is a separate command.
why: The summary exists so reserve stays fast with a large cold ledger (the F-105 design).
Checking the chain on every reserve was judged too slow, and no cheaper binding (a chain-head hash in the index) was added instead.
The ledger tests alter cold segments and then run verify; none alters the summary and then reserves.
findings.root_cause: The fast path takes a file the agent can write as the authority for the cap, and the check that would catch an edit runs only when asked.
findings.sweep: Not swept — deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28). docs/V2-BACKLOG.md lists the fix and the sweep: bind the summary to the chain head and refuse reserve on a mismatch; check every cached total the cap reads.
findings.mechanism_gap: The untrusted-input detectors (hostile-names, mcp F-82 hostile frames) and the archive detector (ledger-archive 'verify catches a lost index, and reserve refuses rather than re-admit') cover names, frames and a lost index; none edits the summary and then calls reserve.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28); docs/V2-BACKLOG.md names the detector to add

findings.title: Secrets are redacted only in a decision's command field; paths and scopes are logged, shown and exported raw
findings.symptom: decisions.jsonl, the console's API and page, and its CSV and JSONL exports redact a secret only in the command text; a secret in a path or scope field appears in full. A secret deny is recorded as rule 'secret' with no fingerprint, and its reason repeats the dispute line twice.
findings.evidence: P0 black-box UAT 2026-10-28 at 8edbc8e, run through the sandboxed runner with a throwaway HOME (findings/reviews/2026-10-28-p0-uat-blackbox.md): cases U-SEC-016/017 (a secret-shaped path shows raw in the API, the page and both exports) and A-ACC-023 (rule 'secret', no fingerprint, the dispute line twice).
findings.direct_cause: Redaction is applied to the command field when a decision is logged; the other string fields are copied unchanged.
why: The secret scan was wired where shell commands are judged, and the command was the field known to carry secrets.
A path or scope can carry a secret too (a file named after a token, an MCP argument).
test/console.test.mjs:763-780 checks redaction with a command field only.
findings.root_cause: The redacted fields are a list of one, where the rule is every string a decision record stores.
findings.sweep: Not swept — deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28). docs/V2-BACKLOG.md lists the fix and the sweep: redact every string field before a decision is written (log, API, page, export), record the fingerprint, print the dispute line once; drive each field with a secret.
findings.mechanism_gap: The partial-list detectors (bundle-absence, claims-are-checked file names, exec-env, the wrapper case) check lists of files and wrappers; none plants a secret in each string field of a decision record, so only the command field was checked.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28); docs/V2-BACKLOG.md names the detector to add

findings.title: The 'read-only' console writes the spend index on a GET, sends no Cache-Control, and checks Origin only on the halt route
findings.symptom: GET /api/try updates the spend day file and file index. No response carries Cache-Control: no-store. API, 403 and 404 responses carry a CSP with an empty nonce. A foreign Origin with a valid token is accepted on GET routes; only POST /api/halt checks it.
findings.evidence: P0 black-box UAT 2026-10-28 at 8edbc8e, run through the sandboxed runner with a throwaway HOME (findings/reviews/2026-10-28-p0-uat-blackbox.md): cases U-SEC-021 (the state tree changes after GET /api/try), U-SEC-022 (no Cache-Control on any response; an empty nonce on API, 403 and 404) and A-ACC-010 (GET /api/overview and /api/records with a foreign Origin and a valid token return 200). specs/console/spec.md:105 claims 'the console was read-only'; spec.md:50 requires Origin for non-GET requests only.
findings.direct_cause: The try route calls the spend reader, which refreshes its index; the header helper builds the CSP per page render and sets no cache header; the Origin check sits in the non-GET branch.
why: 'Read-only' was checked as 'no write route without --allow-halt', not as 'no file changes'.
The spend reader's index refresh is a side effect its callers do not see.
The requirement's cases ask for no-store and an Origin check on every route; the spec narrowed both with no recorded decision.
findings.root_cause: The console states 'read-only' and a header policy that no test checks against the file tree and every response.
findings.sweep: Not swept — deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28). docs/V2-BACKLOG.md lists the fix and the sweep: give the console a spend read without index writes; set no-store and a real CSP on every response; the owner decides Origin on GET; add a test that snapshots the state tree around every GET route.
findings.mechanism_gap: The statement detectors (claims-are-checked: documented codes and file names exist, no 'signed/immutable' claims) check words against code; 'read-only' is not on their list, and no test compares the state tree before and after a GET.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28); docs/V2-BACKLOG.md names the detector to add

findings.title: sakk init prints 'hook wired' but installs no guard, so the one-command setup leaves doctor failing
findings.symptom: sakk init with a cap creates the ledger and ~/.sakk/config.json and prints 'hook wired', but writes nothing to the agent's config; sakk doctor then fails with 'no agent has the guard installed'. init without a cap exits 2.
findings.evidence: P0 black-box UAT 2026-10-28 at 8edbc8e, run through the sandboxed runner with a throwaway HOME (findings/reviews/2026-10-28-p0-uat-blackbox.md): case P-INS-001: init exits 0 printing 'hook wired'; the agent config folder stays empty; doctor exits 1. test/release.test.mjs:177 asserts init's current output, not an installed hook.
findings.direct_cause: init records the ledger in Sakk's own config and leaves guard install to a separate command, while its message says the hook is wired.
why: init and guard install were built in different milestones; the message predates the split.
The release test pins init's text, so the text was never compared with what init does.
The requirement asks for one command that ends in a working guard.
findings.root_cause: A success message states an outcome the command does not produce, and the test pins the message instead of the outcome.
findings.sweep: Not swept — deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28). docs/V2-BACKLOG.md lists the fix and the sweep: make init run guard install, or say it did not and print the next command; assert doctor passes after init; check every 'done' message against the state it claims.
findings.mechanism_gap: The statement detectors check codes and file names in documents; none compares a CLI's success message with the state it claims, so 'hook wired' passed.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28); docs/V2-BACKLOG.md names the detector to add

findings.title: The package ships code derived from MIT-licensed projects without their notices
findings.symptom: src/secret-rules.generated.mjs is ported from gitleaks v8.21.2 (MIT, © Zachary Rice) and src/prices.mjs from LiteLLM's price table (MIT); the package has no NOTICE file and no MIT text for either, and the attribution for cc-safety-net is missing. MIT requires the notice in copies.
findings.evidence: P0 black-box UAT 2026-10-28 at 8edbc8e, run through the sandboxed runner with a throwaway HOME (findings/reviews/2026-10-28-p0-uat-blackbox.md): case P-ACC-008: npm pack --dry-run lists no NOTICE or third-party licence file; grep finds the origin only in code comments.
findings.direct_cause: The port added a provenance comment, and no step in release or pack requires the licence text of a third-party source.
why: Attribution was recorded as provenance (where the data came from), not as a licence obligation.
The release checks cover version, files and tests, not third-party notices.
This blocks the public release, which is the owner's call, so it was held for release day.
findings.root_cause: A licence obligation is a required release step that lives only as rule text, with no check in the release path.
findings.sweep: Not swept — deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28). docs/V2-BACKLOG.md lists the fix and the sweep: add NOTICE with the MIT texts (gitleaks, LiteLLM) and the cc-safety-net attribution, include it in package files, and add a release test that every ported source has its notice. Release blocker.
findings.mechanism_gap: The required-step detectors check the certificate and the self-evolution gate; none lists third-party sources and asserts their notices ship, so the obligation stayed rule text.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28); docs/V2-BACKLOG.md names the detector to add

findings.title: The emittable-code check misses codes written in some source forms, so four reachable refusal codes have no test
findings.symptom: claims-are-checked's EMIT pattern finds codes in its main source forms but not in 'reason: "CODE: …"' strings, nullish defaults or template literals. SPEND_CAP_INVALID (reachable from the hook), HOOK_FAILED, TRY_USAGE and LEDGER_EXPORT_FAILED are emitted but no test asserts them.
findings.evidence: P0 black-box UAT 2026-10-28 at 8edbc8e, run through the sandboxed runner with a throwaway HOME (findings/reviews/2026-10-28-p0-uat-blackbox.md): case A-ACC-006: the hook's SPEND_CAP_INVALID deny is reachable with a non-numeric cap and no test asserts the code; the other three are emitted in the same unrecognised forms.
findings.direct_cause: The EMIT regular expression at test/claims-are-checked.test.mjs:47 lists source forms; a code written another way is not collected, so the 'asserted by a test' check never sees it.
why: The pattern was written from the forms present when the check was added.
Later code used other forms, and the check reports nothing about codes it cannot see.
The check has no control that plants a code in each form and expects it found.
findings.root_cause: The check that every emitted code is tested cannot fail for a code in an unrecognised form — it sees nothing to check.
findings.sweep: Not swept — deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28). docs/V2-BACKLOG.md lists the fix and the sweep: collect codes from every source form (or from a code registry) and add a control per form; write the four missing tests.
findings.mechanism_gap: The can-it-fail detectors (core-specs drill anchors, scorer-rules, claims-are-checked 'every refusal code a source can emit is asserted by at least one test') test the codes the pattern collects; none plants a code in each source form, so the pattern's blind forms went unchecked.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28); docs/V2-BACKLOG.md names the detector to add

findings.title: The console's Stop button reads its token from a cookie the page cannot read, so the halt request is refused and the page hangs
findings.symptom: With --allow-halt, the Stop button reads the session token from document.cookie, but the sakk_t cookie is HttpOnly, so the token is empty and the halt request gets 403. The page does not handle the 403; parsing the response fails and the button stays on '…'.
findings.evidence: P0 black-box UAT 2026-10-28 at 8edbc8e, run through the sandboxed runner with a throwaway HOME (findings/reviews/2026-10-28-p0-uat-blackbox.md): case U-FN-011: in a browser the button sends an empty token and gets 403, and the page throws on the response. The halt route itself works with the token (curl).
findings.direct_cause: The page script reads a cookie the server marks HttpOnly, and the fetch handler assumes a JSON success body.
why: The cookie was made HttpOnly in a later security pass; the page script still reads it.
The console tests call the halt route with curl-style requests that carry the token, not through the page.
No test runs the page's script in a browser.
findings.root_cause: The halt path through the page was never run end to end; the route and the script were each tested alone.
findings.sweep: Not swept — deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28). docs/V2-BACKLOG.md lists the fix and the sweep: send the token the page already holds (from the URL or a non-HttpOnly halt token), handle non-200 replies; add a browser run of the Stop button (part of the C-15 debt plan).
findings.mechanism_gap: The real-path work for this class is the gold v2 debt (REAL-mode cases, F-90/F-112); no detector drives the console page in a browser, so the page-to-route path stayed unrun.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: none: deferred to V2 by the owner (D10, 2026-10-28); docs/V2-BACKLOG.md names the detector to add

findings.title: The classifier recognises a secret read only as a reader command taking the literal filename as a plain operand; every equivalent reading falls through to allow
findings.symptom: A secret file reached through an upload reference, a git version-path or git operand, a move, a remote-copy or mount spec, a credential-printing CLI, or the process-environment pseudo-file classifies as shell.run, net.download or ordinary file words and is allowed; only `<reader> <secret-name>` became secret.read.
findings.evidence: P0 black-box UAT 2026-10-28 at 8edbc8e, run through the sandboxed runner with a throwaway HOME: cases K-SEC-049 (upload reference), K-SEC-050 (credential-printing CLIs, git readings) and K-SEC-051 (process-environment file) all returned allow. Left unfiled at the V1 close (D10); filed 2026-10-29 after D11 unfroze the V2 fix batch (docs/DECISIONS.md).
findings.direct_cause: secret.read is produced in two narrow places — the file.read upgrade in toDecisions and a plain-operand scan in the unmodeled else-branch of the shellActions chain — so any modeled branch, any non-operand spelling and any no-filename credential command bypasses both.
why: The secret-file rule was written for the reader-plus-filename shape the first cases had.
Later widenings (F-153, F-154, F-155) each added one command list instead of restating the rule as 'the spelled-out secret, wherever it appears'.
No test enumerated the readings from the secret's side — every way a command can spell or reach the name — only from the command's side.
findings.root_cause: The recognition is a list of command shapes standing in for the rule: a spelled-out secret name is reached whatever grammar position it occupies, and some commands read credentials with no filename at all, so each reading outside the list escapes until listed.
findings.sweep: Swept the sibling paths in the same commit: plain operands of modeled chain commands (now scanned even when a branch matched), git arguments (a pre-scan before gitActions plus the credential subcommands), mv sources (read before the delete), piece-wise names inside arguments joined by '=', '@' or ':' (upload, mount, remote-copy and version-path specs), and the process-environment file in isSecretPath, so every file.read upgrade in toDecisions (readers, dd, cp, tar, rsync, the Read tool) inherits it. Accepted conservative denials, all fail-closed: git rm --cached or checkout -- on a secret name, a sed script or commit message spelling a secret name next to ':' or '=', and a remote-copy or mount spec whose secret name is only on the remote side.
findings.instance_fix: this commit
findings.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::K-SEC-049/K-SEC-050 a secret filename inside an upload reference, git path, copy or mount is denied
findings.mechanism_gap: The C-02/RC-04 detectors (F-153 movers, F-154 find/xargs, F-155 unmodeled readers) each pin one command list; none enumerates readings from the secret's side, so a reading outside every list — an upload reference, a credential printer, the process environment — escaped all of them.
findings.mechanism_upgrade: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::K-SEC-049 / K-SEC-050 / K-SEC-051: a secret reached by any spelled-out reading is denied (F-203)
